stem: A customer has an active Shield Advanced subscription at the account level. During a volumetric UDP reflection attack targeting an EC2 instance's Elastic IP address used for a custom UDP application, the customer expects enhanced Shield Advanced detection and mitigation metrics in the console but sees none for that resource. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: Elastic IPs aren't eligible for Shield Advanced and get only Standard defenses.
Shield Advanced never inspects UDP traffic, only TCP-based attacks.
A subscription protects everything automatically.
The Elastic IP was never added as a protected resource.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced protects only resources explicitly added as protected resources. The Elastic IP wasn't added.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EIPs ineligible: they're eligible.
• No UDP inspection: UDP attacks are covered.
• Automatic coverage: must add resources.

Key takeaway: add each resource to Shield Advanced.

stem: Instances in a private subnet can successfully initiate outbound HTTPS connections to an external API, and security group rules correctly allow the outbound request and its stateful return traffic. Connections still fail, however. The subnet's network ACL has an inbound rule allowing TCP port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 and an outbound rule allowing TCP port 443 to 0.0.0.0/0, with all other traffic implicitly denied. What is the cause?

choices.text: NACLs support only outbound rules, so inbound rules are ignored for private subnets.
Security groups are stateless and need an explicit inbound rule for responses.
NACL rules are evaluated in reverse order.
NACLs are stateless; allow inbound ephemeral ports for the replies.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NACLs are stateless, so responses to outbound requests need inbound rules for ephemeral ports.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Outbound only: NACLs have both.
• SGs stateless: they're stateful.
• Reverse order: lowest number first.

Key takeaway: stateless NACLs need return-port rules.

stem: An app tier accepts traffic only from a web tier. Both scale dynamically across 3 AZs, and IPs change constantly. Which rule fits?

choices.text: Reference the web SG ID in the app subnet's NACL
App SG inbound: allow the web tier's security group
Add each web instance IP as a /32 rule
Allow the whole VPC CIDR in the app tier SG

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security group references allow traffic from any ENI in the referenced group, regardless of IP, so scaling needs no rule changes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Whole VPC CIDR: too broad.
• NACL SG reference: NACLs can't reference security groups.
• /32 per instance: breaks with scaling and hits rule limits.

Key takeaway: reference security groups, not IPs.

stem: A network engineer adds a new NACL rule with rule number 50 that denies inbound traffic from a specific malicious CIDR block. Shortly after, legitimate traffic from an unrelated, previously allowed CIDR range starts being blocked as well. The existing allow rule for that legitimate range has rule number 100. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: Lowest number first; rule 50 matched the legitimate range too.
Rule 50 applies only to outbound traffic.
Adding any deny rule inverts the default action for every other rule in the ACL.
NACLs evaluate all matching rules and apply the most restrictive one.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NACL rules are evaluated lowest number first and the first match applies. Rule 50's range also covered legitimate traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Outbound only: it's inbound.
• Inverts defaults: no.
• Most restrictive: first match wins.

Key takeaway: check NACL deny ranges and order.

stem: A security team needs to allow inbound access from over 200 corporate office CIDR ranges to a fleet of application servers, but the default security group rule quota per security group makes maintaining individual CIDR rules impractical, and they also want to update every associated security group in one place when office ranges change. What should they implement?

choices.text: A customer-managed prefix list referenced in one rule.
Request an unlimited rule quota and keep adding each CIDR as its own rule.
Use a NACL instead, since NACLs allow unlimited CIDR rules with no quota.
Create 200 security groups, one per CIDR, and attach them all to every instance.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A customer-managed prefix list holds all 200 CIDRs and is referenced in one security group rule, staying within quotas and easy to update.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Unlimited rules: quotas exist.
• NACLs unlimited: also limited and stateless.
• 200 SGs: impractical.

Key takeaway: many CIDRs → prefix lists.

stem: A security team enables VPC Flow Logs to capture all rejected traffic for a subnet containing EC2 instances that resolve internal hostnames using the VPC's Amazon-provided DNS resolver. During an audit, they cannot find any flow log records showing DNS queries from the instances to that resolver, even though other traffic is logged correctly. What is the reason?

choices.text: Flow logs exclude Amazon DNS traffic; use Resolver query logging.
The 10-minute aggregation interval is too long to capture short DNS flows.
DNS uses UDP, and flow logs capture only TCP traffic by default.
DNS is excluded unless the custom format includes a dns-query field.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Flow logs don't capture traffic to the Amazon DNS resolver. Use Resolver query logging for DNS visibility.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Interval too long: not the reason.
• UDP excluded: flow logs include UDP.
• dns-query field: doesn't exist.

Key takeaway: DNS visibility → Resolver query logs.

stem: Traffic from EC2 instances in a private subnet passes through a NAT gateway before reaching the internet. Default-format VPC Flow Logs for the NAT gateway's ENI show the NAT gateway's own IP address as both srcaddr and dstaddr for translated flows, making it impossible to identify which private instance originated a suspicious outbound connection. How should the team reconfigure flow logs to solve this?

choices.text: Enable flow logs on each instance's ENI, since instance-level logs ignore NAT.
A custom format with pkt-srcaddr and pkt-dstaddr.
Set a 1-minute aggregation interval so pre-NAT addresses are captured.
Send flow logs to CloudWatch Logs.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A custom flow log format with pkt-srcaddr and pkt-dstaddr shows the original instance addresses behind the NAT gateway.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Instance ENI logs only: doesn't show post-NAT.
• 1-minute interval: unrelated.
• CloudWatch destination: unrelated.

Key takeaway: NAT visibility → pkt-* fields.

stem: A security team stores VPC Flow Logs in Amazon S3 in Parquet format and wants to identify potential port-scanning activity, characterized by a single source IP address generating many REJECT-action records against numerous distinct destination ports on the same destination IP within a short time window. Which approach detects this pattern at scale without building custom log-processing infrastructure?

choices.text: Have GuardDuty disable delivery, since Athena can't query Parquet flow logs.
Download and search each file manually for REJECT and count matches per file.
Athena SQL on REJECTs, counting distinct ports per source in a window.
Enable WAF logging on the VPC.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Athena can query Parquet flow logs with SQL, counting distinct destination ports per source among REJECTs in a time window to find scans.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Athena can't query Parquet: it can.
• Manual file search: impractical.
• WAF logging: HTTP only.

Key takeaway: detect port scans with Athena.

stem: An auditor asks whether AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress and CreateVpc calls are captured by a trail with default settings, and for how long they're queryable without a trail. Which answer is correct?

choices.text: Neither is logged unless data events are enabled
Only CreateVpc is logged by default; security group changes need data events
Both are management events; event history keeps 90 days
VPC API calls appear only in VPC Flow Logs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Both calls change resource configuration, so they are management events logged by default. CloudTrail event history shows 90 days of management events even without a trail; a trail stores them long-term.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Data events: those are object- or item-level operations.
• Only CreateVpc: both are management events.
• Flow logs: capture traffic, not API calls.

Key takeaway: configuration changes = management events.

stem: A central security account expects to see CloudTrail records for a VPC peering connection acceptance (ec2:AcceptVpcPeeringConnection) performed in a member account's ap-southeast-2 region, but the organization trail configured in the management account shows no such event. The organization trail was created as a single-region trail in us-east-1. What is the issue?

choices.text: The trail is single-Region; make it multi-Region (and organization-wide).
Organization trails can't capture EC2 networking events, only IAM events.
The member account must enable its own trail, since org trails skip networking calls.
Peering acceptance is logged only in the requester's Region, here us-east-1.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A single-Region trail misses events from other Regions. Make it multi-Region (and organization-wide).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Org trails can't capture EC2 networking: they can.
• Member must have own trail: org trails cover members.
• Requester's Region only: acceptance is logged where it happens.

Key takeaway: multi-Region trails capture all Regions.

stem: A company wants to automatically revoke any inbound security group rule that opens port 3389 (RDP) to 0.0.0.0/0 within seconds of it being created, using near real-time detection of the API call rather than periodic compliance scans. Which architecture best achieves this?

choices.text: Enable GuardDuty, wait for an UnauthorizedAccess finding.
A Config rule on a 24-hour periodic trigger with SSM Automation remediation.
Use VPC Flow Logs to detect RDP traffic and remediate after a connection is seen.
EventBridge on AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress invoking a revoking Lambda.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule on AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress invokes a Lambda function that revokes port 3389 rules immediately.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Wait for GuardDuty: exposure remains.
• 24-hour Config rule: slow.
• Flow logs: only after traffic.

Key takeaway: prevent exposure windows → event-driven remediation.

stem: The compliance team wants continuous evaluation of security groups for SSH open to 0.0.0.0/0, with automatic removal of the bad rule across the organization. Which setup fits?

choices.text: Amazon Inspector network reachability findings reviewed each week
restricted-ssh via conformance pack, with SSM remediation
Trusted Advisor cost checks
CloudTrail Insights on security group changes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The managed Config rule restricted-ssh evaluates security groups continuously. Deployed org-wide (for example, in a conformance pack) with automatic remediation via an SSM document, it removes the offending rule.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inspector reachability: assessment, not continuous compliance with remediation.
• Trusted Advisor cost checks: wrong category.
• CloudTrail Insights: anomaly detection.

Key takeaway: continuous config compliance + fix → Config rule + remediation.

stem: An organization needs an AWS Config rule that evaluates whether every VPC in the account has an associated AWS Network Firewall firewall attached to its route tables, a check with no equivalent AWS managed Config rule. How should they implement this?

choices.text: This validation isn't possible with AWS Config and must be done manually.
A custom Lambda-backed Config rule using EC2 and Network Firewall APIs.
Conformance packs only, which express any custom logic in YAML without Lambda.
A managed Config rule built specifically for Network Firewall route checks.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A custom Lambda-backed Config rule can call EC2 and Network Firewall APIs to check whether each VPC has an associated firewall.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Not possible with Config: custom rules make it possible.
• Conformance packs express any logic: no.
• Managed rule for this: none built specifically.

Key takeaway: custom checks → custom Config rules.

stem: A Config rule correctly evaluates overly permissive network ACL entries as NON_COMPLIANT, and this status is visible in the AWS Config console, but non-compliant resources are never automatically corrected. The security team expected automatic remediation. What is missing from the configuration?

choices.text: No remediation action is attached; add an SSM document and enable auto-remediation.
Convert the rule to a managed rule, since custom rules can't use remediation.
Automatic remediation also requires Security Hub, since Config can't invoke SSM.
Config rules are read-only and can never trigger remediation of any kind.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Remediation happens only if a remediation action (such as an SSM Automation document) is attached and automatic remediation is enabled.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Custom rules can't remediate: they can.
• Needs Security Hub: no.
• Config read-only: remediation actions exist.

Key takeaway: attach a remediation action.

stem: Requirement 1: verify VPC configurations against internal rules continuously. Requirement 2: detect instances communicating with known malicious IPs. Which pairing fits?

choices.text: Security Hub alone for both, with no other service
GuardDuty for requirement 1; Config for requirement 2
Config for both, with custom rules on traffic
Config for requirement 1; GuardDuty for requirement 2

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Config evaluates resource configuration against rules. GuardDuty analyzes VPC traffic, DNS, and CloudTrail data against threat intelligence to detect malicious activity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Swapped: each service in the other's role.
• Config for traffic: Config doesn't analyze traffic.
• Security Hub alone: aggregates findings; it relies on services like Config and GuardDuty.

Key takeaway: configuration → Config; behavior and threats → GuardDuty.

stem: GuardDuty reports UnauthorizedAccess:EC2/MaliciousIPCaller for an instance. What does it indicate, and what is a sound first response?

choices.text: An IAM user signed in from a Tor exit node
WAF blocked a malicious HTTP request to it
Its security group was changed by an unauthorized user
It is talking to a threat-listed IP; isolate and investigate

explanation:
Why this is correct:
This finding means the instance is communicating with an IP on a threat intelligence list. Isolate it (for example, swap to a restrictive security group), preserve evidence, and investigate with Detective.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG changed: that would appear as a different finding or event type.
• WAF block: not a GuardDuty finding.
• Tor sign-in: a different IAM-related finding.

Key takeaway: read the finding type to know what was observed, then contain and preserve evidence.

stem: A security team wants to detect whether a compromised EC2 instance is beaconing to known command-and-control (C2) infrastructure without deploying any host-based agent or manually configuring threat intelligence feeds. Which capability should they rely on?

choices.text: GuardDuty (traffic, DNS, and CloudTrail vs. threat intel; agentless).
Manual flow log review, since GuardDuty needs a paid third-party threat feed.
Network Firewall Suricata rules only.
Inspector network reachability analysis, built to detect C2 beaconing.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty analyzes VPC flow logs, DNS logs, and CloudTrail against threat intelligence, without agents, to detect C2 beaconing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Needs third-party feed: built-in.
• Network Firewall only: requires rule management.
• Inspector: vulnerabilities.

Key takeaway: C2 detection → GuardDuty.

stem: A team enables Amazon GuardDuty for the first time and is concerned it will not detect network-based threats because their VPCs do not have VPC Flow Logs enabled, assuming GuardDuty consumes the customer's own flow log delivery to S3 or CloudWatch. Is this concern valid?

choices.text: Yes; GuardDuty requires flow logs delivered to an S3 bucket that it polls.
No; GuardDuty reads these data sources on its own, independently.
No; GuardDuty analyzes only CloudTrail management events, not network traffic.
Yes; Resolver DNS query logging must be enabled before any network findings.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty consumes flow log, DNS, and CloudTrail data independently. You don't need to enable those logs yourself.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Requires flow logs to S3: no.
• Only CloudTrail: no.
• Resolver logging required: no.

Key takeaway: GuardDuty reads its own data sources.

stem: An EC2 instance is configured to send all DNS queries to a third-party DNS resolver over the internet instead of using the VPC's default Amazon-provided DNS resolver. The security team relies on GuardDuty to detect DNS-based data exfiltration (such as Trojan:EC2/DNSDataExfiltration) from this instance. What is the impact?

choices.text: Only VPC Flow Logs are affected; GuardDuty's DNS capture is resolver-independent.
Bypassing the Amazon resolver hides its DNS queries from GuardDuty.
No impact; GuardDuty inspects DNS packets at the ENI regardless of resolver.
GuardDuty redirects the instance's DNS traffic back to the Amazon resolver.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty sees DNS queries through the Amazon-provided resolver. Sending queries to a third-party resolver hides them from GuardDuty's DNS analysis.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only flow logs affected: DNS analysis is affected.
• Inspects at the ENI: no.
• Redirects DNS: no.

Key takeaway: bypassing the VPC resolver reduces visibility.

stem: A VPN connection has two tunnels. The customer device keeps only tunnel 1 up, and during AWS maintenance traffic dropped. What should the customer do?

choices.text: Configure both tunnels (BGP preferred) so one takes over
Configure only tunnel 2 as a manual backup that the NOC brings up
Use the second tunnel for IPv6 only
Request that AWS skip maintenance on tunnel 1

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The two tunnels terminate on different AWS endpoints for redundancy. AWS may take one tunnel down for maintenance, so both must be configured, ideally with BGP, so traffic fails over automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual backup: slow and error-prone.
• IPv6-only tunnel: not the purpose of the second tunnel.
• Skipping maintenance: not an option.

Key takeaway: always configure both VPN tunnels.

stem: A financial services company must ensure that its AWS Site-to-Site VPN connections use only AES-256 encryption, SHA-2 hashing, and IKEv2 with a minimum Diffie-Hellman group of 14, per internal cryptographic standards, rather than accepting AWS's default proposal set that also allows weaker options for backward compatibility. How should this be enforced?

choices.text: Set tunnel options to only the approved algorithms, DH groups, and IKE version.
Restrict them on the customer gateway only, since AWS tunnel options can't be customized.
A Config rule blocking weak tunnels, since tunnel options aren't in the VPN API.
Use defaults, since the VPN only ever negotiates AES-256, SHA-2, and IKEv2.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Set the AWS tunnel options to allow only the approved encryption, integrity algorithms, DH groups, and IKE versions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CGW only: AWS side may accept weaker ones.
• Config rule blocking tunnels: not the mechanism.
• Defaults only AES-256: defaults include others.

Key takeaway: enforce crypto via tunnel options.

stem: An AWS Site-to-Site VPN tunnel repeatedly transitions between UP and DOWN states every few minutes, even though the customer gateway device shows the Phase 1 and Phase 2 IPsec security associations as established. The administrator confirms Dead Peer Detection (DPD) is enabled on the customer gateway with a shorter interval than what AWS negotiated. What is the most likely cause of the flapping?

choices.text: Mismatched DPD timers; align timeout and retry settings.
The tunnel exceeds its throughput limit, which AWS handles by cycling it.
Tunnels have a five-minute maximum session and reconnect continuously by design.
The customer gateway IP changed.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Frequent UP/DOWN cycling often comes from mismatched DPD timers. Align timeouts and retries on both sides.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Throughput limit: drops packets, not tunnels.
• Five-minute sessions: no.
• CGW IP change: tunnel wouldn't come back.

Key takeaway: flapping tunnels → check DPD.

stem: A company has a 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection and needs all traffic across it encrypted in transit to meet a regulatory requirement. They are evaluating (1) an IPsec Site-to-Site VPN over a public or transit virtual interface on top of Direct Connect, versus (2) enabling MACsec directly on the Direct Connect connection. What is a key tradeoff between these approaches?

choices.text: VPN over DX caps per-tunnel throughput; MACsec runs near line rate.
VPN always outperforms MACsec, since VPN is Layer 2 and MACsec is Layer 3.
Both give identical throughput and latency, so choose on cost alone.
MACsec can't be used on Direct Connect.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
VPN over DX is limited per tunnel (about 1.25 Gbps). MACsec encrypts at near line rate on supported dedicated connections.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPN outperforms MACsec: no.
• Identical: no.
• MACsec unavailable on DX: it's available.

Key takeaway: line-rate DX encryption → MACsec.

stem: A customer orders a 10 Gbps hosted Direct Connect connection from an AWS Direct Connect Partner and attempts to enable MACsec encryption through the AWS console, but the option is unavailable. What is the reason, and what should the customer do?

choices.text: The Direct Connect Partner must submit a separate AWS Support case per hosted connection to unlock MACsec, after which it behaves identically to a dedicated connection.
MACsec is not supported on hosted connections regardless of speed; the customer must order a dedicated connection directly from AWS at an eligible speed to use MACsec.
MACsec requires the customer to enable it on the AWS side first, after which it automatically propagates to hosted connections within 24 hours.
MACsec is unavailable because the connection is below 100 Gbps; only 100 Gbps connections of any type, hosted or dedicated, support MACsec.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
MACsec isn't supported on hosted connections. It requires a supported dedicated connection.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Partner support case: no.
• Enable on AWS side first: still unsupported.
• Below 100 Gbps: 10 Gbps dedicated supports it.

Key takeaway: MACsec → dedicated connections.

stem: To operationally support MACsec on a dedicated Direct Connect connection, a network security team needs to understand how encryption keys are established and maintained between the customer router and the AWS Direct Connect device. Which statement correctly describes this process?

choices.text: AWS generates and manages all MACsec keys; CKN and CAK aren't used.
Keys must be re-entered in the console at each rotation.
A CKN/CAK pre-shared pair; MKA derives and rotates data keys.
MACsec uses the same TLS certificate-based key exchange as ACM certificates.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
MACsec uses a pre-shared CKN/CAK pair, and MKA derives and rotates the data encryption keys.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS manages all keys: you supply CKN/CAK.
• Re-enter at each rotation: MKA handles rotation.
• TLS certificates: not used.

Key takeaway: MACsec keys = CKN/CAK + MKA.

stem: A platform team is implementing mutual TLS (mTLS) between internal microservices running in a private VPC, where each service must present a client certificate issued by a certificate authority trusted only within the organization, without exposing any certificate authority information publicly or relying on a public CA. Which service should they use to establish and operate this private PKI hierarchy?

choices.text: Public ACM, which issues certificates for private hostnames after DNS validation.
Cognito user pool client certificates for service-to-service authentication.
Secrets Manager's built-in CA, purpose-built for mTLS client certificates.
AWS Private CA (ACM Private CA).

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Private CA issues private certificates for internal mTLS between services.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public ACM for private hostnames: not allowed.
• Cognito client certificates: no.
• Secrets Manager CA: doesn't exist.

Key takeaway: internal mTLS → Private CA.

stem: A team requests a public ACM certificate for use with an Application Load Balancer and wants the certificate to renew automatically without manual intervention indefinitely, as long as the underlying domain configuration remains unchanged. Which validation method should they choose, and why?

choices.text: Either method renews identically.
DNS validation, renewed automatically while the CNAME remains.
HTTP validation, since ALB certificates renew only when validated by an HTTP token.
Email validation, the only method that renews without any customer action.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DNS validation renews automatically as long as the validation CNAME stays in DNS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identical renewal: email needs action.
• HTTP validation for ALB: not the ACM method here.
• Email renews without action: it needs approval.

Key takeaway: auto-renewing ACM → DNS validation.

stem: An ACM public certificate used by a CloudFront distribution fails to renew automatically, and the ACM console shows the certificate as Expired shortly after its validity period ended. The certificate was originally issued using DNS validation. Investigation reveals that the CNAME validation record in Route 53 was deleted several months ago during a DNS cleanup effort. What is the correct explanation and remediation?

choices.text: Certificates need no ongoing validation, so it's a CloudFront certificate cache issue.
Deleting the CNAME affects only HTTP-validated certificates, not DNS-validated ones.
Renewal needs the validation CNAME; recreate it or reissue.
ACM falls back to email validation.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DNS-validated ACM renewal needs the validation CNAME. Recreate it, or reissue the certificate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No ongoing validation: renewal validates again.
• Only HTTP-validated: no.
• Falls back to email: not automatically.

Key takeaway: keep validation CNAMEs.

stem: A company needs certificates for two distinct use cases: (1) a public-facing website validated via a domain name it owns and that is resolvable on the internet, and (2) internal services identified only by private, non-internet-resolvable hostnames used strictly within a VPC. Which statement correctly compares the appropriate certificate sources for these two cases?

choices.text: Private CA for both, since public ACM certificates are being deprecated.
Public ACM for both, since validation is optional for internal hostnames.
Private CA can issue only IP-address certificates.
Public ACM for the website; Private CA for internal hostnames.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Use public ACM certificates for the public website and AWS Private CA for internal hostnames.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Private CA for both: browsers won't trust it.
• Public ACM for internal names: validation isn't optional.
• IP-only certificates: no.

Key takeaway: public names → ACM; internal → Private CA.

stem: A healthcare company must send data containing protected health information (PHI) to a third-party SaaS analytics platform that also runs on AWS, and its compliance policy prohibits this traffic from traversing the public internet at any point, even if encrypted with TLS. Which architecture satisfies this confidentiality requirement?

choices.text: A public ACM certificate with TLS 1.3 over the internet, which satisfies any path rule.
An internet gateway with security groups restricted to the provider's IP ranges.
Global Accelerator anycast IPs, considered part of the AWS private network.
AWS PrivateLink to the provider's endpoint service.
The provider's public API endpoint.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
PrivateLink to the provider's endpoint service keeps PHI traffic on the AWS network without internet exposure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• TLS over internet: still internet.
• IGW with SGs: internet.
• Global Accelerator: public entry points.
• Public endpoint: internet.

Key takeaway: private third-party access → PrivateLink.

stem: A team creates an interface VPC endpoint for a service and enables the private DNS option, expecting that application calls to the service's standard public hostname will now resolve to the endpoint's private IP addresses. However, applications in the VPC continue to reach the service over the internet via its public IP addresses. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: Interface endpoints never override public DNS.
The VPC's enableDnsSupport/enableDnsHostnames aren't both enabled.
The endpoint's security group must allow outbound internet traffic for private DNS.
Private DNS for interface endpoints affects only Lambda traffic, not EC2 instances.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Private DNS for interface endpoints requires the VPC's enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames attributes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Never override: private DNS does.
• SG outbound internet: no.
• Only Lambda: no.

Key takeaway: private DNS needs VPC DNS attributes.

stem: A SaaS provider offers customers two connectivity options to reach its multi-tenant service running in its own VPC: VPC peering or an AWS PrivateLink endpoint service. From a security and network isolation perspective, why would the SaaS provider prefer to offer PrivateLink rather than VPC peering to its customers?

choices.text: Identical security; PrivateLink simply has no data processing charges.
Peering is more secure, since it uses IPsec by default and PrivateLink is unencrypted.
Peering scales better, with unlimited transitive peering across customer VPCs.
PrivateLink exposes only the service, not full VPC reachability.

explanation:
## Two ways to reach a service in another VPC
- **VPC peering** connects two whole networks. Once routes are added, any resource in one VPC can try to reach any IP in the other; only security groups and network ACLs limit it.
- **AWS PrivateLink** connects to one service. The provider puts the service behind a Network Load Balancer and publishes it as an endpoint service. The customer creates an interface endpoint: a network interface with an IP from the customer's own CIDR. The customer's apps talk to that local IP, and AWS carries the traffic privately to the service.
## Why this matters for a SaaS provider
With peering, every customer VPC becomes routable to the provider's VPC and vice versa, so one misconfigured security group could expose other systems. Peering also requires non-overlapping CIDRs, which is hard to guarantee across hundreds of customers.
With PrivateLink, connections can only be opened from the customer to the one published service, the provider's VPC is never routable, and overlapping CIDRs do not matter because no routing between the VPCs happens.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Same security, just cheaper:** the security model is different (one service versus a whole network), and PrivateLink is not free. It charges per endpoint-hour and per GB processed.
- ✗ **B. Peering uses IPsec:** VPC peering does not build IPsec tunnels, and PrivateLink traffic stays on the AWS network where applications add TLS as usual. Encryption is not what separates the two options; reachability is.
- ✗ **C. Peering scales better:** VPC peering is not transitive, each peering is a separate one-to-one connection with its own routes, and CIDRs must not overlap. That scales worse than one endpoint service that any number of customers can connect to.
- ✓ **D. PrivateLink exposes only the service (correct):** customers reach one endpoint, not the provider's network, so the blast radius is limited to that service and connections flow only from consumer to provider.

## Key idea
Peering connects networks (IP ranges must be unique and everything becomes routable); PrivateLink exposes one service (overlap does not matter and nothing else is reachable).

stem: A VPC Flow Log record shows source 203.0.113.5, destination 10.0.1.20, srcport 443, dstport 51000, protocol 6 (TCP), action REJECT. The instance owning the destination ENI has a security group allowing inbound TCP on ephemeral ports from anywhere. What is the most likely reason this traffic was rejected, and what should the analyst check next?

choices.text: The security group is stateless and blocked the return traffic; make it stateful.
Flow logs never record REJECT for traffic a security group allows, so this is a logging error.
Likely the NACL; flow logs don't say which layer rejected.
The traffic was blocked automatically by AWS Shield Advanced.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Return traffic to an ephemeral port was rejected. Security groups are stateful and allow it, so the likely cause is a NACL. Flow logs don't say which layer rejected.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG stateless: false.
• Never REJECT when SG allows: NACL can reject.
• Shield blocked it: not how flow logs show it.

Key takeaway: REJECT on return traffic → suspect NACLs.

stem: During an incident investigation, a security team suspects that CloudTrail log files stored in S3 may have been tampered with after delivery. The trail was configured with log file validation enabled from creation. What should the team do to verify whether any log files were modified or deleted after delivery?

choices.text: Compare S3 object ETags manually with values shown in the CloudTrail console
Run aws cloudtrail validate-logs for the time range
Re-download CloudTrail Insights events
Enable GuardDuty, which retroactively validates historical log file integrity

explanation:
Why this is correct:
aws cloudtrail validate-logs checks the digest chain to prove whether log files were modified or deleted.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual ETag comparison: not reliable.
• Insights events: unrelated.
• GuardDuty retroactive validation: no.

Key takeaway: prove log integrity → validate-logs.

stem: A company serves an API behind Amazon CloudFront and AWS WAF (CLOUDFRONT scope). After enabling the AWS Managed Rules SQL Database rule group, legitimate JSON requests containing a business field named 'SELECT_PLAN' are being blocked. The security team must eliminate the false positives while keeping SQL injection protection active for all other traffic. What should they do?

choices.text: Remove the SQL database managed rule group from the web ACL entirely
Replace WAF with Shield Advanced
Switch the web ACL scope from CLOUDFRONT to REGIONAL to change evaluation
Override only the offending rule's action to Count

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Overriding only the offending rule's action to Count stops false positives while keeping the rest of the managed rule group active.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove the whole group: loses protection.
• Shield Advanced: not a WAF rule fix.
• Change scope: not how it works.

Key takeaway: false positives → override one rule.

stem: During a Layer 7 DDoS attack against a CloudFront distribution, an organization's AWS bill spikes sharply due to origin auto-scaling triggered by the attack traffic. The distribution is protected by Shield Advanced and associated with a AWS WAF web ACL. Which requirement determines whether the organization is eligible for Shield Advanced's DDoS cost protection for the resulting scaling charges?

choices.text: Charges must stem from a DDoS on a Shield Advanced-protected resource
The account needs Enterprise Support and a signed Business Associate Agreement
Cost protection applies only if Route 53 health checks were disabled during the event
The DRT must have pre-approved the architecture in writing before the attack

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DDoS cost protection applies to charges caused by a DDoS on a Shield Advanced-protected resource. Request credits through Support.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Enterprise Support and BAA: not required.
• Health checks disabled: unrelated.
• DRT pre-approval: not required.

Key takeaway: cost protection only for protected resources.

stem: Two Transit Gateways in us-east-1 and eu-west-1 are connected by an inter-Region peering attachment. VPC routes propagate correctly within each Region, but VPCs cannot reach VPCs in the other Region. What is the MOST likely missing configuration?

choices.text: Static routes to the remote CIDRs via the peering attachment.
The peering attachment must be configured to use jumbo frames.
BGP must be enabled on the peering attachment.
A Direct Connect gateway must be associated with both Transit Gateways.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
TGW peering doesn't support propagation. Add static routes to remote CIDRs pointing to the peering attachment in each TGW route table.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Jumbo frames: unrelated.
• BGP on peering: not supported.
• DX gateway: unrelated.

Key takeaway: TGW peering = static routes.

stem: A company has one Direct Connect connection in Frankfurt and 80 VPCs attached to Transit Gateways in eu-central-1 and eu-west-1. It wants on-premises access to all VPCs over this connection with the fewest virtual interfaces. Which design fits BEST?

choices.text: One private VIF per VPC on the Frankfurt connection.
VPC peering from a single VPC that holds the private VIF.
One transit VIF to a DX gateway on both TGWs.
One public VIF with VPN tunnels to each VPC.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
One transit VIF to a Direct Connect gateway associated with the Transit Gateways gives all 80 VPCs access over one connection.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VIF per VPC: VIF limits.
• Peering via one VPC: not transitive.
• Public VIF with VPN tunnels: complex.

Key takeaway: many VPCs over DX → transit VIF + DX gateway + TGW.

stem: A SaaS provider must expose one TCP service to hundreds of customer VPCs. Many customers use overlapping CIDR ranges such as 10.0.0.0/16, and customers must not gain access to any other provider resources. Which solution fits BEST?

choices.text: Public IP addresses restricted by security groups per customer.
A Transit Gateway shared with all customers through AWS RAM.
A PrivateLink endpoint service behind an NLB.
VPC peering with each customer VPC and restrictive security groups.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A PrivateLink endpoint service behind an NLB works with overlapping customer CIDRs and exposes only the TCP service.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public IPs: internet exposure.
• Shared TGW: overlapping CIDRs break routing.
• Peering: overlapping CIDRs not allowed.

Key takeaway: overlapping consumers → PrivateLink.

stem: A website uses CloudFront with an S3 origin in us-east-1. If that origin returns 5xx errors or times out, CloudFront should automatically fetch from a replicated bucket in us-west-2. Which configuration achieves this?

choices.text: Increase the origin connection timeout and attempts.
An origin group with primary and secondary origins and failover status codes.
Two separate distributions with Route 53 failover between them.
Lambda@Edge that rewrites every request to the secondary bucket.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An origin group with primary and secondary origins fails over automatically on 5xx errors or timeouts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer timeouts: still fails.
• Two distributions with DNS: slower.
• Lambda@Edge rewrite: always uses secondary.

Key takeaway: CloudFront origin failover → origin groups.

stem: Security wants to block VPC workloads from resolving known malicious domains and newly registered domains, and to log every blocked query, across 50 accounts. Which solution fits BEST?

choices.text: Route 53 public hosted zones created for each malicious domain.
Network ACLs that block the IP addresses of malicious domains.
DNS Firewall managed lists via Firewall Manager, with logging.
Security group outbound rules that restrict port 53.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DNS Firewall with AWS managed domain lists (malware, newly registered domains), deployed org-wide via Firewall Manager with logging, blocks resolution centrally.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public zones per domain: nonsense.
• NACLs by IP: IPs change.
• SG port 53: blocks all DNS.

Key takeaway: block malicious resolution org-wide → DNS Firewall + Firewall Manager.

stem: A company has two Direct Connect connections, A and B, both advertising the same on-premises prefix. It wants AWS to prefer connection A for traffic from the VPCs to on premises, with B as backup. Which approach achieves this?

choices.text: Tag connection A's prefix with 7224:7300.
Advertise the prefix over connection B with the community 7224:7300.
Advertise a less specific prefix over connection A than over B.
Set a higher MED on the prefix advertised over connection A.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The 7224:7300 community sets high local preference in AWS, making AWS prefer connection A for traffic to that prefix.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Community on B: wrong connection.
• Less specific on A: makes B preferred.
• Higher MED on A: makes A less preferred.

Key takeaway: prefer a DX path → 7224:7300 community.

stem: A company has a dedicated 100 Gbps Direct Connect connection and must encrypt traffic at line rate between its router and the AWS device without the throughput limits of IPsec. Which option fits BEST?

choices.text: MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) on the dedicated connection.
A private IP VPN with a single IPsec tunnel over the connection.
TLS at the application layer only, for every service that uses the link.
Site-to-Site VPN over a public virtual interface.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
MACsec on a dedicated 100 Gbps connection encrypts at line rate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Single IPsec tunnel: throughput limited.
• Application TLS only: not all traffic.
• VPN over public VIF: throughput limited.

Key takeaway: line-rate encryption → MACsec.

stem: A branch connects to AWS with a Site-to-Site VPN, but the workload needs about 4 Gbps and a single tunnel is capped near 1.25 Gbps. Which approach increases aggregate throughput?

choices.text: Enable acceleration on the existing VPN connection only.
Terminate the VPN on a virtual private gateway and raise the MTU.
Multiple BGP-routed VPN connections on a Transit Gateway with ECMP enabled.
Static routing on one VPN connection with both tunnels active.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Multiple BGP-routed VPN connections on a Transit Gateway with ECMP spread traffic beyond the per-tunnel limit.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Acceleration alone: doesn't raise per-tunnel limit.
• VGW: no ECMP across connections.
• Static routing: no ECMP.

Key takeaway: VPN throughput → ECMP on TGW.

stem: After an acquisition, application VPC A (10.1.0.0/16) must call an API in VPC B, which uses the same CIDR. Renumbering is not possible soon. Which option enables the call with the least complexity?

choices.text: A Transit Gateway attachment for both VPCs with route propagation.
Add a secondary CIDR to VPC A and leave the workloads in place.
VPC peering between A and B with specific routes.
PrivateLink: an endpoint service in B, endpoint in A.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With overlapping CIDRs, PrivateLink (endpoint service in B, interface endpoint in A) exposes the API without routing between the VPCs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• TGW propagation: overlapping routes.
• Secondary CIDR alone: workloads still overlap.
• Peering: not allowed with overlaps.

Key takeaway: overlapping networks → PrivateLink.

stem: IPv6-enabled instances in a VPC must be able to download updates from the internet over IPv6, but must not accept inbound connections initiated from the internet. Which component provides this?

choices.text: A NAT gateway in a public subnet.
A virtual private gateway.
An egress-only internet gateway.
An internet gateway with no security group rules.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An egress-only internet gateway allows outbound IPv6 connections and blocks inbound connections initiated from the internet.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NAT gateway: IPv4 (NAT64 aside).
• VGW: VPN.
• IGW: allows inbound.

Key takeaway: IPv6 outbound only → egress-only IGW.

stem: An instance in one VPC cannot connect to a database in another VPC over a Transit Gateway. Several teams manage route tables, security groups, and NACLs. Which tool identifies the blocking component fastest without sending traffic?

choices.text: VPC Flow Logs.
Traffic Mirroring.
VPC Reachability Analyzer.
CloudWatch Network Monitor synthetic probes.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Reachability Analyzer traces the configured path across SGs, NACLs, route tables, and TGW, identifying the blocking component.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flow Logs: show results, not cause.
• Traffic Mirroring: packets.
• Network Monitor: latency and loss.

Key takeaway: find the blocking config → Reachability Analyzer.

stem: A security team wants to run an out-of-band intrusion detection system that inspects full packet payloads from selected EC2 instances without placing an inline appliance. Which feature fits BEST?

choices.text: VPC Flow Logs with all available fields enabled.
CloudTrail data events for the selected instances.
Gateway Load Balancer inline inspection of all traffic.
VPC Traffic Mirroring to a Network Load Balancer in front of the IDS fleet.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Traffic Mirroring copies full packets to an NLB fronting the IDS, out of band.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flow Logs: metadata only.
• CloudTrail: API calls.
• GWLB inline: not out of band.

Key takeaway: out-of-band payload inspection → Traffic Mirroring.

stem: Flow logs on a NAT gateway's network interface show the NAT gateway's private IP as the source for outbound traffic, so the team cannot tell which instance generated suspicious connections. Which change helps?

choices.text: Enable Traffic Mirroring on the NAT gateway's interface.
Enable flow logs on the internet gateway.
A custom format with pkt-srcaddr/pkt-dstaddr.
Replace the NAT gateway with a public NAT instance.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A custom format with pkt-srcaddr and pkt-dstaddr shows the original instance IPs and final destinations through the NAT gateway.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Mirroring the NAT gateway: not supported.
• IGW flow logs: not available.
• NAT instance: unnecessary.

Key takeaway: see behind NAT → pkt-* fields.

stem: Instances in two VPCs use an MTU of 9001. Large packets between them are dropped when traffic flows through a Transit Gateway, while small packets succeed. What explains this?

choices.text: Jumbo frames work only across VPC peering in different Regions.
Security groups drop fragmented packets between VPCs.
Transit Gateway supports a maximum MTU of 8500 bytes, so larger packets drop.
Transit Gateway supports only a 1500-byte MTU for all traffic.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transit Gateway supports a maximum MTU of 8500 bytes. 9001-byte packets are dropped (or need PMTUD).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Jumbo only cross-Region peering: no.
• SGs drop fragments: no.
• 1500 only: TGW supports 8500.

Key takeaway: TGW MTU = 8500.

stem: Private subnets in three Availability Zones all route internet traffic through a single NAT gateway in AZ a. The team wants to reduce cross-AZ data transfer charges and remove the single-AZ dependency. What should it do?

choices.text: Move all instances to AZ a next to the NAT gateway.
A NAT gateway in each AZ, with each private route table pointing to its local one.
Increase the NAT gateway's bandwidth allocation.
Replace the NAT gateway with an egress-only internet gateway.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A NAT gateway in each AZ, with each AZ's route table pointing to its local NAT gateway, removes the single-AZ dependency and cross-AZ charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Move instances to one AZ: loses resilience.
• More bandwidth: still single AZ.
• Egress-only IGW: IPv6 only.

Key takeaway: NAT gateway per AZ.

stem: A regulated company must inspect encrypted outbound HTTPS traffic for data exfiltration patterns within AWS, using a centrally managed firewall. Which capability fits BEST?

choices.text: VPC Flow Logs analysis of outbound connections.
AWS Network Firewall with TLS inspection using ACM certificates.
Security groups with outbound rules per destination.
Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall domain lists.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Network Firewall TLS inspection decrypts outbound HTTPS using ACM certificates, inspects it, and re-encrypts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flow logs: no payload.
• SGs: no inspection.
• DNS Firewall: domains only.

Key takeaway: inspect encrypted traffic → Network Firewall TLS inspection.

stem: Partner systems call an API behind an ALB. The company requires that only clients presenting certificates issued by its private CA can connect, with certificate validation done at the load balancer. Which solution fits BEST?

choices.text: WAF IP allow lists for each partner's addresses.
API keys sent in a custom header on each request.
A Network Load Balancer with TCP passthrough and no validation.
ALB mTLS (verify mode) with the private CA in a trust store.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ALB mutual TLS in verify mode, with the private CA in a trust store, accepts only clients with valid certificates.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IP allow lists: not identity.
• API keys: not certificates.
• NLB passthrough without validation: doesn't verify.

Key takeaway: client certificate enforcement → ALB mTLS.

stem: A company wants to guarantee that VPCs in selected accounts cannot send or receive traffic through internet gateways, while allowing specific exempted subnets that host public load balancers. Which feature fits BEST?

choices.text: Security groups with no inbound rules in each VPC.
An SCP that denies ec2:CreateInternetGateway.
VPC Block Public Access with subnet exclusions.
Network ACLs in every subnet denying internet traffic.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
VPC Block Public Access blocks internet traffic for VPCs in the account (with subnet exclusions if needed), regardless of gateways or routes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No inbound SG rules: outbound still possible.
• SCP on creating IGWs: existing ones remain.
• NACLs everywhere: error-prone.

Key takeaway: guarantee no internet → VPC Block Public Access.

stem: Microservices across 30 accounts and many VPCs must call each other over HTTP, with service-level authorization based on the calling IAM principal, and without managing VPC peering or Transit Gateway routing. Which service fits BEST?

choices.text: A Transit Gateway with network ACLs between VPCs.
Public ALBs protected by AWS WAF.
VPC peering between all VPCs with security groups.
VPC Lattice with IAM auth policies.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
VPC Lattice connects services across accounts and VPCs with service-level IAM auth policies, without managing network routing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• TGW with NACLs: no service-level auth.
• Public ALBs: internet exposure.
• Peering mesh: no service auth.

Key takeaway: cross-account service-to-service → VPC Lattice.

stem: A public API is a frequent target of layer 7 DDoS attacks. The company wants automatic mitigation rules created during attacks, access to the AWS Shield Response Team, and protection against scaling charges caused by attacks. Which solution fits BEST?

choices.text: Auto Scaling with a very high maximum capacity.
Shield Advanced with auto L7 mitigation via WAF.
Network ACLs with rate limits on the subnets.
AWS Shield Standard only.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced automatic application layer DDoS mitigation creates and manages WAF rules during attacks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More scaling: absorbs costly traffic.
• NACL rate limits: not supported.
• Shield Standard: no L7 automation.

Key takeaway: automatic L7 mitigation → Shield Advanced.

stem: A global application serves users over TCP and UDP and needs two static anycast IP addresses with automatic failover between Regional endpoints. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Global Accelerator
Amazon CloudFront with origin groups
An internet-facing Application Load Balancer
Route 53 latency-based routing records

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs and routes TCP and UDP to healthy Regional endpoints over the AWS network.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon CloudFront with origin groups: CloudFront focuses on HTTP(S) and does not provide static anycast IPs for UDP.
• An internet-facing Application Load Balancer: An ALB is Regional and HTTP only.
• Route 53 latency-based routing records: DNS routing returns changing IPs and depends on TTLs.

Key takeaway: Static anycast IPs for TCP/UDP → Global Accelerator.

stem: A media company serves large video files from S3 to viewers worldwide and wants to reduce load on the origin from many edge locations. Which CloudFront feature helps most?

choices.text: Signed cookies for every public viewer
Field-level encryption on all requests
Geo restriction for all viewer countries
Origin Shield in a Region close to the origin

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Origin Shield adds a central caching layer that consolidates requests from edge locations to the origin.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Signed cookies for every public viewer: Signed cookies control access, not origin load.
• Field-level encryption on all requests: Field-level encryption protects specific fields.
• Geo restriction for all viewer countries: Geo restriction blocks countries.

Key takeaway: Reduce origin load across edges → Origin Shield.

stem: A CloudFront distribution must serve private S3 content so that users cannot bypass CloudFront to reach the bucket. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: A security group on the S3 bucket allowing CloudFront IPs
S3 static website hosting with public read access enabled on the bucket
A public bucket with obscure object names for each file
Origin access control with a bucket policy allowing only the distribution

explanation:
Why this is correct:
OAC signs CloudFront requests to S3, and the bucket policy allows only that distribution.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A security group on the S3 bucket allowing…: S3 buckets do not use security groups.
• S3 static website hosting with public read…: Public website hosting exposes content.
• A public bucket with obscure object names…: Obscure names are not access control.

Key takeaway: Lock S3 origins to CloudFront with OAC.

stem: A company wants simple request header manipulation and URL rewrites at the edge with sub-millisecond execution at the lowest cost. Which option fits?

choices.text: CloudFront Functions
Lambda@Edge functions
ALB listener rule sets
AWS WAF managed rules

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront Functions run lightweight JavaScript at edge locations with very low latency and cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda@Edge functions: Lambda@Edge suits heavier logic and costs more.
• ALB listener rule sets: ALB rules run in a Region, not at the edge.
• AWS WAF managed rules: WAF filters requests but does not rewrite URLs.

Key takeaway: Lightweight edge logic → CloudFront Functions.

stem: On-premises servers must resolve names in Route 53 private hosted zones associated with VPCs. Which component is required?

choices.text: A Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint in the VPC
An internet gateway attached to the VPC
A Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint in the VPC
A public hosted zone with the same domain name

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inbound endpoints receive DNS queries from on-premises resolvers for private zones.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An internet gateway attached to the VPC: IGWs do not provide DNS resolution for on-premises.
• A Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint in the VPC: Outbound endpoints forward queries from the VPC to on-premises.
• A public hosted zone with the same domain name: Public zones expose records publicly.

Key takeaway: On-premises to AWS private DNS → inbound endpoint.

stem: Workloads in 30 VPCs across accounts must resolve an on-premises domain. The company wants one set of Resolver endpoints. Which design fits?

choices.text: Public hosted zones replicating all of the on-premises records for each VPC
Custom DNS servers on EC2 in every VPC forwarding queries over the internet
Outbound endpoints deployed in every one of the 30 VPCs, with forwarding rules created separately in each account
Outbound endpoints in a shared services VPC with forwarding rules shared through RAM and associated with each VPC

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Resolver rules can be shared with RAM and associated with many VPCs while using centralized endpoints.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public hosted zones replicating all of the…: Public zones expose internal records.
• Custom DNS servers on EC2 in every VPC…: EC2 DNS servers add management and internet exposure.
• Outbound endpoints deployed in every one of…: Per-VPC endpoints add cost and management.

Key takeaway: Centralize hybrid DNS with shared Resolver rules.

stem: A private hosted zone in Account A must be used by a VPC in Account B. Which steps are required?

choices.text: Peer the two VPCs and rely on the peering connection to share private DNS resolution automatically
Make the hosted zone public so Account B can resolve the names
Copy all records into a new private zone in Account B manually
Create an association authorization in Account A, then associate the VPC from Account B

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account private zone association requires authorization from the zone owner and association by the VPC owner.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Peer the two VPCs and rely on the peering…: Peering alone does not share private zones.
• Make the hosted zone public so Account B can…: Public zones expose records.
• Copy all records into a new private zone in…: Manual copies drift.

Key takeaway: Cross-account private zones need authorization plus association.

stem: A company must protect its public DNS zone against spoofed responses. Which feature fits?

choices.text: DNSSEC signing on the Route 53 public hosted zone
Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rule groups
Route 53 weighted routing records
Route 53 private hosted zones only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DNSSEC signing lets resolvers validate that responses are authentic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rule groups: DNS Firewall filters outbound queries from VPCs.
• Route 53 weighted routing records: Weighted routing distributes traffic.
• Route 53 private hosted zones only: Private zones are internal.

Key takeaway: Authenticate DNS responses with DNSSEC.

stem: An application uses a custom TCP protocol and must preserve client source IP addresses to the targets. Which load balancer fits?

choices.text: Classic Load Balancer
Application Load Balancer
Gateway Load Balancer
Network Load Balancer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NLB handles TCP and UDP at layer 4 and can preserve client source IPs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Classic Load Balancer: Classic is legacy.
• Application Load Balancer: ALB is for HTTP(S).
• Gateway Load Balancer: GWLB is for virtual appliances.

Key takeaway: Custom TCP with client IP preservation → NLB.

stem: A fleet of third-party firewall appliances must inspect traffic transparently and scale horizontally. Which load balancer fits?

choices.text: Gateway Load Balancer using GENEVE encapsulation
Application Load Balancer with path-based rules
Classic Load Balancer with sticky sessions
Network Load Balancer with TLS termination

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gateway Load Balancer distributes traffic to appliances transparently using GENEVE.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Application Load Balancer with path-based rules: ALB is for HTTP routing.
• Classic Load Balancer with sticky sessions: Classic is legacy.
• Network Load Balancer with TLS termination: NLB does not provide transparent insertion.

Key takeaway: Scale inline appliances with Gateway Load Balancer.

stem: An HTTPS application must route requests to different services based on host headers and URL paths. Which load balancer fits?

choices.text: Application Load Balancer
Network Load Balancer
AWS Global Accelerator
Gateway Load Balancer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ALB supports host- and path-based routing rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Network Load Balancer: NLB does not inspect HTTP.
• AWS Global Accelerator: Global Accelerator does not route by path.
• Gateway Load Balancer: GWLB is for appliances.

Key takeaway: Host and path routing → ALB.

stem: Behind an NLB with TLS passthrough, targets need the original client IP, and client IP preservation cannot be used. Which feature helps?

choices.text: X-Forwarded-For headers from the NLB
Sticky sessions on the target group
Cross-zone load balancing enabled
Proxy protocol v2 on the target group

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Proxy protocol v2 prepends connection information, including the client IP, for targets to read.

Why the other options are wrong:
• X-Forwarded-For headers from the NLB: NLB does not add HTTP headers.
• Sticky sessions on the target group: Stickiness does not convey IPs.
• Cross-zone load balancing enabled: Cross-zone balancing does not convey IPs.

Key takeaway: Pass client IPs through NLB with proxy protocol v2.

stem: A team must capture metadata about accepted and rejected traffic in a VPC for troubleshooting security groups. Which feature fits?

choices.text: CloudTrail data events
Route 53 query logs
VPC Traffic Mirroring
VPC Flow Logs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Flow Logs record IP traffic metadata, including accept and reject decisions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail data events: CloudTrail records API calls.
• Route 53 query logs: Query logs record DNS queries.
• VPC Traffic Mirroring: Traffic Mirroring copies full packets.

Key takeaway: Traffic metadata → VPC Flow Logs.

stem: A security team must inspect full packet payloads from specific EC2 instances with an intrusion detection appliance. Which feature fits?

choices.text: VPC Traffic Mirroring
VPC Reachability Analyzer
VPC Flow Logs
CloudWatch Internet Monitor

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Traffic Mirroring copies packets from network interfaces to monitoring appliances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC Reachability Analyzer: Reachability Analyzer checks configuration paths.
• VPC Flow Logs: Flow Logs capture metadata only.
• CloudWatch Internet Monitor: Internet Monitor measures internet performance.

Key takeaway: Full packet inspection → Traffic Mirroring.

stem: A company wants visibility into internet performance and availability issues affecting its users of CloudFront and VPC-hosted applications. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon CloudWatch Internet Monitor
IAM Access Analyzer findings
AWS Trusted Advisor checks
AWS Config advanced queries

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Internet Monitor shows how internet issues affect application performance and availability for users.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM Access Analyzer findings: Access Analyzer reviews access.
• AWS Trusted Advisor checks: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations.
• AWS Config advanced queries: Config queries configuration.

Key takeaway: Internet impact visibility → Internet Monitor.

stem: A company needs 20 Gbps of dedicated private connectivity to AWS with resilience against a single device failure. Which design fits?

choices.text: Two Site-to-Site VPN tunnels over one internet connection
A single 100 Gbps Direct Connect connection terminated at one location only, with no second path
Two or more Direct Connect connections at different locations, optionally bundled in LAGs
One hosted Direct Connect connection of 50 Mbps capacity

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Redundant connections at diverse locations provide capacity and resilience.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Two Site-to-Site VPN tunnels over one…: VPN over one internet link lacks dedicated capacity.
• A single 100 Gbps Direct Connect connection…: A single connection is a single point of failure.
• One hosted Direct Connect connection of 50…: 50 Mbps is far too small.

Key takeaway: Resilient DX → multiple connections at diverse locations.

stem: An on-premises network must reach VPCs in three Regions over Direct Connect using transit gateways. Which virtual interface type fits?

choices.text: Hosted private VIF to an S3 endpoint
Public virtual interface to the internet
Private virtual interface to a single VPC's gateway
Transit virtual interface to a Direct Connect gateway

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transit VIFs connect to DX gateways associated with transit gateways in multiple Regions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hosted private VIF to an S3 endpoint: Private VIFs do not target S3 endpoints.
• Public virtual interface to the internet: Public VIFs reach public AWS endpoints.
• Private virtual interface to a single VPC's…: A private VIF to one VPC does not scale across Regions.

Key takeaway: DX to transit gateways → transit VIF.

stem: With two Direct Connect connections, the company wants on-premises outbound traffic to prefer connection A and use B only as backup. Which BGP attribute should be set on the on-premises routers?

choices.text: Lower AS_PATH length advertised to AWS over connection B
A shorter prefix advertised over connection B to AWS
Higher local preference for routes learned over connection A
A higher MED sent to AWS on connection A only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Local preference influences outbound path selection from the on-premises side.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lower AS_PATH length advertised to AWS over…: AS_PATH advertised to AWS affects inbound traffic from AWS.
• A shorter prefix advertised over connection…: Prefix length toward AWS affects AWS's choice, not outbound.
• A higher MED sent to AWS on connection A only: MED toward AWS affects AWS's choice, not on-premises outbound.

Key takeaway: Control your outbound path with local preference.

stem: The company wants AWS to send return traffic over the primary Direct Connect connection rather than the backup. Which technique fits?

choices.text: Shut down BGP on the primary connection during peak hours
Advertise the same prefix only through the VPN connection
Increase local preference on the on-premises routers for the primary only
Prepend AS_PATH on routes advertised over the backup connection

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Longer AS_PATHs over the backup make AWS prefer the primary for return traffic (with equal prefix lengths).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shut down BGP on the primary connection…: Shutting BGP removes the primary.
• Advertise the same prefix only through the…: VPN-only advertising removes DX use.
• Increase local preference on the on-premises…: Local preference affects on-premises outbound.

Key takeaway: Influence AWS return paths with AS_PATH prepending.

stem: A company needs fast failure detection on Direct Connect BGP sessions so traffic moves to backup within about a second. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD)
Longer BGP hold timers on sessions
Jumbo frames on the private VIF
Static routes instead of BGP sessions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
BFD detects link failures quickly, triggering faster BGP failover.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer BGP hold timers on sessions: Longer timers slow detection.
• Jumbo frames on the private VIF: Jumbo frames affect MTU.
• Static routes instead of BGP sessions: Static routes do not detect failures.

Key takeaway: Fast DX failover → BFD.

stem: A company needs encrypted connectivity over Direct Connect for compliance. Which TWO options provide encryption? (Select TWO)

choices.text: BGP communities on advertised prefixes only
A public VIF with no additional configuration
Site-to-Site VPN running over Direct Connect
Jumbo frames enabled on the virtual interface
MACsec on supported dedicated connections

explanation:
Why this is correct:
MACsec encrypts at layer 2 on supported connections, and VPN over DX encrypts at the IP layer.

Why the other options are wrong:
• BGP communities on advertised prefixes only: Communities influence routing.
• A public VIF with no additional configuration: A public VIF alone is not encrypted.
• Jumbo frames enabled on the virtual interface: MTU settings do not encrypt.

Key takeaway: Encrypt DX with MACsec or VPN over DX.

stem: A company has 200 VPCs in one Region across many accounts and wants transitive routing with segmentation between environments. Which design fits?

choices.text: A transit gateway with separate route tables for each environment
A full mesh of VPC peering connections between all 200 of the VPCs
One VPC with 200 subnets shared by every account
Site-to-Site VPN connections between every pair of VPCs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transit gateway route tables provide transitive routing and segmentation at scale.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A full mesh of VPC peering connections…: Peering is non-transitive and unmanageable at this scale.
• One VPC with 200 subnets shared by every account: One giant VPC lacks isolation.
• Site-to-Site VPN connections between every…: Pairwise VPNs are unmanageable.

Key takeaway: Scale and segment VPC routing with transit gateway route tables.

stem: Two VPCs need high-bandwidth, low-latency connectivity with no transitive routing requirement and no hourly attachment fees. Which option fits?

choices.text: Direct Connect
Transit gateway
Site-to-Site VPN
VPC peering

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Peering connects two VPCs directly without attachment charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Direct Connect: Direct Connect connects on-premises networks.
• Transit gateway: Transit gateways add attachment and processing fees.
• Site-to-Site VPN: VPN has lower throughput.

Key takeaway: Simple two-VPC connectivity → peering.

stem: Stateful firewall appliances in an inspection VPC attached to a transit gateway drop return traffic because flows are asymmetric across AZs. Which setting fixes this?

choices.text: Disable route propagation on every attachment
Add more subnets to the inspection VPC in one AZ
Enable DNS support on the transit gateway
Enable appliance mode on the inspection VPC attachment

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Appliance mode keeps both directions of a flow on the same AZ attachment, preserving symmetry.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable route propagation on every attachment: Disabling propagation breaks routing.
• Add more subnets to the inspection VPC in one AZ: More subnets in one AZ do not fix symmetry.
• Enable DNS support on the transit gateway: DNS support is unrelated.

Key takeaway: Symmetric inspection through TGW → appliance mode.

stem: A company connects transit gateways in two Regions. What is true about routing across the peering attachment?

choices.text: Routes propagate dynamically across peering with BGP automatically
Peering attachments only support IPv6 traffic between Regions
Routes across the peering attachment must be added as static routes
Peering requires a Direct Connect gateway between the Regions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transit gateway peering attachments use static routes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Routes propagate dynamically across peering…: Dynamic propagation across peering is not supported this way.
• Peering attachments only support IPv6…: IPv4 is supported.
• Peering requires a Direct Connect gateway…: A DX gateway is not required.

Key takeaway: TGW peering uses static routes.

stem: A company must connect SD-WAN appliances in a VPC to a transit gateway with dynamic routing and higher throughput than VPN. Which attachment fits?

choices.text: Transit Gateway Connect attachment using GRE and BGP
A Site-to-Site VPN with static routing only
A private VIF directly to the SD-WAN VPC
A VPC peering connection with static routes to the appliances

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Connect attachments use GRE tunnels with BGP for SD-WAN integration and high throughput.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A Site-to-Site VPN with static routing only: Static VPN lacks dynamic routing and has lower throughput.
• A private VIF directly to the SD-WAN VPC: A private VIF is on-premises connectivity.
• A VPC peering connection with static routes…: Peering does not integrate SD-WAN with dynamic routing to TGW.

Key takeaway: SD-WAN integration with TGW → Connect attachments.

stem: A company must manage a global network spanning several Regions and on-premises sites with centralized policy-based segments. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Cloud WAN
VPC peering mesh
Amazon Route 53
AWS VPN CloudHub

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cloud WAN builds and manages global networks with policy-defined segments.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC peering mesh: A peering mesh does not scale or segment.
• Amazon Route 53: Route 53 is DNS.
• AWS VPN CloudHub: CloudHub connects VPN sites through a VGW.

Key takeaway: Policy-driven global networking → Cloud WAN.

stem: Service-to-service communication across many VPCs and accounts needs application-layer networking with auth policies and no need for route management. Which service fits?

choices.text: VPC peering mesh
NAT gateways only
Amazon VPC Lattice
Site-to-Site VPN

explanation:
Why this is correct:
VPC Lattice connects services across VPCs and accounts with built-in auth policies and without managing routes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC peering mesh: Peering requires routing and does not provide service auth.
• NAT gateways only: NAT gateways provide egress.
• Site-to-Site VPN: VPN is network-level connectivity.

Key takeaway: Service networking without route management → VPC Lattice.

stem: Which TWO options provide backup connectivity if a single Direct Connect connection fails? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A larger VPC CIDR block in the Region
A second internet gateway on the same VPC
More NAT gateways in each private subnet
A second Direct Connect connection at another location
A Site-to-Site VPN connection as a backup path

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Additional DX connections or VPN backups keep hybrid connectivity during failures.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A larger VPC CIDR block in the Region: CIDR size is unrelated.
• A second internet gateway on the same VPC: A VPC has only one internet gateway.
• More NAT gateways in each private subnet: NAT gateways are for internet egress.

Key takeaway: Back up DX with DX or VPN.

stem: A company needs to restrict content in CloudFront to viewers in specific countries. Which feature fits?

choices.text: CloudFront geographic restrictions
CloudFront Origin Shield
CloudFront real-time logs
CloudFront field-level encryption

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Geographic restrictions allow or block viewers by country.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFront Origin Shield: Origin Shield reduces origin load.
• CloudFront real-time logs: Real-time logs record requests.
• CloudFront field-level encryption: Field-level encryption protects specific fields.

Key takeaway: Country-based access → geo restriction.

stem: A company wants to block VPC workloads from resolving known malicious domains. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Route 53 public DNSSEC
Route 53 traffic flow
Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall
Route 53 health checks

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DNS Firewall filters outbound DNS queries from VPCs using domain lists.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route 53 public DNSSEC: DNSSEC signs public zones.
• Route 53 traffic flow: Traffic flow manages routing policies.
• Route 53 health checks: Health checks monitor endpoints.

Key takeaway: Block malicious domains from VPCs → DNS Firewall.

stem: An ALB serves traffic across three AZs, but one AZ has fewer targets and becomes overloaded. Which setting spreads requests evenly across all targets?

choices.text: Sticky sessions per target
Slow start on targets
Deregistration delay
Cross-zone load balancing

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-zone load balancing distributes requests across targets in all enabled AZs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Sticky sessions per target: Stickiness pins users to targets.
• Slow start on targets: Slow start ramps new targets.
• Deregistration delay: Deregistration delay drains connections.

Key takeaway: Even distribution across AZs → cross-zone load balancing.

stem: A team wants to verify whether an EC2 instance can reach a database, and identify the blocking component, without sending traffic. Which tool fits?

choices.text: AWS Config snapshots
VPC Reachability Analyzer
VPC Traffic Mirroring
Amazon Inspector scans

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Reachability Analyzer analyzes configurations to determine reachability and identify blocking components.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Config snapshots: Config snapshots record configuration.
• VPC Traffic Mirroring: Traffic Mirroring copies packets.
• Amazon Inspector scans: Inspector finds vulnerabilities.

Key takeaway: Configuration-based path analysis → Reachability Analyzer.

stem: Users far from the only Region hosting an HTTP API report high latency on dynamic requests that cannot be cached. Which TWO options can reduce latency? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Enabling S3 Transfer Acceleration on an unrelated bucket
Increasing the API's instance sizes in the single Region that hosts it
Setting a longer DNS TTL for the API's hostname
Global Accelerator to route traffic onto the AWS network near users
CloudFront in front of the API to use persistent connections from edge locations

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Both services bring users onto the AWS network close to them, reducing latency for dynamic traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Enabling S3 Transfer Acceleration on an…: S3 acceleration is unrelated to the API.
• Increasing the API's instance sizes in the…: Larger instances do not reduce network distance.
• Setting a longer DNS TTL for the API's hostname: DNS TTL does not affect request latency.

Key takeaway: Accelerate dynamic traffic with CloudFront or Global Accelerator.
