stem: A company sets up a Site-to-Site VPN with dynamic routing. What must the customer gateway device support?

choices.text: Static routes only, configured once on a single tunnel
GRE tunnels only, without any IPsec encryption support
IPsec tunnels and BGP sessions over both tunnels
MACsec encryption on a dedicated fiber cross-connect

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Dynamic VPNs use IPsec tunnels with BGP to exchange routes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Static routes only, configured once on a…: Static routing does not provide dynamic routing, and a single tunnel lacks redundancy.
• GRE tunnels only, without any IPsec…: AWS VPN requires IPsec.
• MACsec encryption on a dedicated fiber…: MACsec applies to Direct Connect.

Key takeaway: Dynamic VPN → IPsec plus BGP.

stem: A single VPN connection to a transit gateway is limited in throughput. The company needs more aggregate bandwidth over VPN. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Multiple VPN connections with ECMP enabled on the transit gateway
Static routes on a single tunnel with a higher priority configured
Disabling the second tunnel so all traffic uses only the first tunnel
One VPN connection to a virtual private gateway with larger MTU values

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ECMP on a transit gateway spreads traffic across multiple VPN tunnels for more bandwidth.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Static routes on a single tunnel with a…: Static priority does not aggregate bandwidth.
• Disabling the second tunnel so all traffic…: Disabling tunnels reduces capacity and redundancy.
• One VPN connection to a virtual private…: VGWs do not support ECMP across connections this way, and MTU does not add bandwidth.

Key takeaway: Aggregate VPN bandwidth with ECMP on TGW.

stem: Remote offices connect over VPN from locations with poor internet paths to AWS. Which option improves VPN performance?

choices.text: A second VPC with its own virtual private gateway
Disabling BGP to use only static routes on tunnels
Accelerated Site-to-Site VPN using Global Accelerator
A larger instance size for the customer gateway router

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Accelerated VPN enters the AWS network at the nearest edge location, improving performance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A second VPC with its own virtual private…: Another VPC does not improve paths.
• Disabling BGP to use only static routes on…: Static routing does not improve performance.
• A larger instance size for the customer…: Router size does not fix internet path quality.

Key takeaway: Improve VPN paths with accelerated VPN.

stem: A company must create a private VIF on a hosted Direct Connect connection provided by a partner. Which step must the company perform?

choices.text: Accept the hosted connection or hosted VIF in its account, then configure BGP
Order a new dedicated port from AWS and wait for the letter of authorization
Create a public VIF and advertise all company prefixes to the internet
Attach an internet gateway to the VPC before the VIF can come up

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Hosted connections and VIFs are provisioned by partners and accepted by the customer, followed by BGP configuration.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Order a new dedicated port from AWS and wait…: Hosted connections do not require ordering a dedicated port.
• Create a public VIF and advertise all…: A public VIF is not the requirement.
• Attach an internet gateway to the VPC before…: IGWs are unrelated.

Key takeaway: Accept hosted connections, then configure BGP.

stem: Two dedicated Direct Connect connections at the same location should behave as one logical link with combined bandwidth. Which feature fits?

choices.text: A transit virtual interface
A link aggregation group (LAG)
A hosted virtual interface
A Direct Connect gateway

explanation:
Why this is correct:
LAGs bundle multiple connections at the same location into one logical connection.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A transit virtual interface: Transit VIFs connect to DX gateways.
• A hosted virtual interface: Hosted VIFs are partner-provided interfaces.
• A Direct Connect gateway: DX gateways connect to VPCs or transit gateways.

Key takeaway: Bundle DX ports with LAGs.

stem: A private VIF is configured, but the BGP session stays in Idle. Which TWO issues are the most likely causes? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Missing route table entry in a public subnet
An S3 bucket policy denying the router's access
Security group blocking outbound HTTPS traffic
Mismatched BGP ASN or peer IP addresses
Incorrect MD5 authentication key

explanation:
Why this is correct:
BGP sessions fail to establish when ASNs, peer IPs, or MD5 keys do not match.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Missing route table entry in a public subnet: Route tables do not stop BGP sessions from forming.
• An S3 bucket policy denying the router's access: Bucket policies are unrelated.
• Security group blocking outbound HTTPS traffic: Security groups do not affect DX BGP.

Key takeaway: Check ASNs, peer IPs, and MD5 keys when BGP is down.

stem: How many prefixes can the customer advertise to AWS over a private VIF before the BGP session goes down?

choices.text: Unlimited prefixes
Up to 1 prefix only
Up to 10 prefixes
Up to 100 prefixes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A private VIF accepts up to 100 advertised prefixes from the customer; exceeding this puts the session into idle.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Unlimited prefixes: There is a limit.
• Up to 1 prefix only: Multiple prefixes are allowed.
• Up to 10 prefixes: The limit is higher.

Key takeaway: Summarize routes to stay under DX prefix limits.

stem: A company attaches 50 VPCs to a transit gateway. Production VPCs must reach shared services but not development VPCs. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: One route table associated with every attachment and propagating all routes from all VPCs
Separate route tables for production and development, both propagating shared services routes
Network ACLs in shared services that deny all production traffic by default
Security groups on every instance blocking development CIDR ranges manually

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Associations and propagations per route table control which VPCs can reach each other.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One route table associated with every…: One route table allows all-to-all routing.
• Network ACLs in shared services that deny…: Denying production traffic breaks the requirement.
• Security groups on every instance blocking…: Instance-level blocking is error-prone.

Key takeaway: Segment TGW routing with route tables.

stem: A transit gateway must be used by VPCs in many accounts of the same organization. How should it be shared?

choices.text: Share it through AWS Resource Access Manager
Share IAM access keys for the owner account
Peer every VPC with the TGW owner's VPC
Create a copy of it in every member account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RAM shares transit gateways with accounts or OUs so they can attach their VPCs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Share IAM access keys for the owner account: Sharing keys is insecure.
• Peer every VPC with the TGW owner's VPC: Peering does not attach to TGWs.
• Create a copy of it in every member account: Separate TGWs fragment routing.

Key takeaway: Share TGWs with RAM.

stem: Two peered VPCs cannot communicate although the peering connection is active. Which TWO items must be checked? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Both VPCs use the same DHCP options set
Both VPCs have internet gateways attached
Security groups and NACLs allow the traffic
Both VPCs have NAT gateways deployed
Route tables in both VPCs point to the peering connection

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Peering requires routes on both sides and permissive security rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both VPCs use the same DHCP options set: DHCP options do not block peering traffic.
• Both VPCs have internet gateways attached: IGWs are not needed for peering.
• Both VPCs have NAT gateways deployed: NAT gateways are not needed.

Key takeaway: Peering needs routes and security rules on both sides.

stem: A VPC needs more IP addresses because its original CIDR is nearly exhausted. What is the least disruptive option?

choices.text: Resize existing subnets in place to use more addresses
Add a secondary CIDR block to the VPC and create new subnets
Delete the VPC and recreate it with a larger primary CIDR block
Assign public IPs to all instances to free private IPs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Secondary CIDR blocks expand VPC address space without rebuilding.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Resize existing subnets in place to use more…: Existing subnet sizes cannot be changed.
• Delete the VPC and recreate it with a larger…: Recreating the VPC is disruptive.
• Assign public IPs to all instances to free…: Public IPs do not free private addresses.

Key takeaway: Expand VPCs with secondary CIDRs.

stem: A company wants to plan, allocate, and track IP address space across accounts and Regions to avoid overlapping CIDRs. Which service fits?

choices.text: Route 53 Resolver query logging
AWS Config aggregators by account
VPC Flow Logs in each account
Amazon VPC IP Address Manager (IPAM)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IPAM manages IP pools, allocation, and monitoring across accounts and Regions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route 53 Resolver query logging: Query logs record DNS queries.
• AWS Config aggregators by account: Config aggregates configuration data.
• VPC Flow Logs in each account: Flow Logs record traffic.

Key takeaway: Organization-wide IP planning → IPAM.

stem: Many security groups and route tables reference the same set of partner CIDRs that change occasionally. Which feature simplifies management?

choices.text: Managed prefix lists
VPC endpoint policies
DHCP option sets
Elastic IP pools

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Prefix lists group CIDRs and can be referenced in security groups and route tables, updated in one place.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC endpoint policies: Endpoint policies control endpoint access.
• DHCP option sets: DHCP options configure DNS and domain settings.
• Elastic IP pools: Elastic IPs are public addresses.

Key takeaway: Manage shared CIDR sets with prefix lists.

stem: Private subnets in two VPCs with overlapping CIDRs must reach a shared service through a transit gateway. Which option allows this?

choices.text: Internet gateways in both VPCs with public addresses for all instances
Direct VPC peering between each of the overlapping VPCs and the shared service VPC
Private NAT gateways translating the overlapping ranges to non-overlapping ones
A single transit gateway route table containing both overlapping CIDRs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Private NAT gateways translate source addresses so overlapping networks can reach shared resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Internet gateways in both VPCs with public…: Public exposure is unnecessary and insecure.
• Direct VPC peering between each of the…: Peering fails with overlapping CIDRs.
• A single transit gateway route table…: Overlapping routes conflict.

Key takeaway: Work around overlapping CIDRs with private NAT.

stem: VPC workloads must resolve corp.example.com using on-premises DNS servers. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: A DHCP options set pointing only to the AmazonProvidedDNS server
A Resolver outbound endpoint with a forwarding rule for corp.example.com
A public hosted zone named corp.example.com with copied records
A Resolver inbound endpoint with a system rule for corp.example.com

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Outbound endpoints forward queries for specified domains to on-premises DNS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A DHCP options set pointing only to the…: AmazonProvidedDNS alone cannot resolve on-premises names.
• A public hosted zone named corp.example.com…: Public zones expose internal names.
• A Resolver inbound endpoint with a system…: Inbound endpoints accept queries from on-premises.

Key takeaway: VPC to on-premises DNS → outbound endpoint plus forwarding rule.

stem: Both on-premises and AWS must resolve each other's private names. Which TWO components are required? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Internet gateways attached to every VPC in the design
Public IP addresses for all DNS resolvers on premises
Public hosted zones with all private records copied
Resolver outbound endpoints with forwarding rules to on-premises
Resolver inbound endpoints for on-premises queries to AWS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Hybrid DNS needs inbound endpoints for on-premises-to-AWS queries and outbound endpoints for AWS-to-on-premises queries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Internet gateways attached to every VPC in…: IGWs are unrelated.
• Public IP addresses for all DNS resolvers on…: Public resolver IPs are unnecessary.
• Public hosted zones with all private records…: Public zones expose records.

Key takeaway: Hybrid DNS needs both inbound and outbound endpoints.

stem: A company wants to log DNS queries made by resources in its VPCs for security analysis. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Route 53 Resolver query logging
Route 53 traffic flow policies
Route 53 public DNSSEC signing
Route 53 health check alarms

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Resolver query logging records DNS queries from VPCs to CloudWatch Logs, S3, or Firehose.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route 53 traffic flow policies: Traffic flow manages routing.
• Route 53 public DNSSEC signing: DNSSEC signs public zones.
• Route 53 health check alarms: Health checks monitor endpoints.

Key takeaway: Log VPC DNS queries with Resolver query logging.

stem: An on-premises DNS server forwards queries for a private hosted zone to a Resolver inbound endpoint, but queries fail. Which TWO checks are most relevant? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The VPC's DNS support attribute is disabled for security
The inbound endpoint is placed in a subnet without routes
The private hosted zone is associated with the VPC containing the inbound endpoint
The private hosted zone is converted to a public hosted zone for on-premises use
Security groups on the inbound endpoint allow DNS traffic from on-premises

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The zone must be associated with the endpoint's VPC, and endpoint security groups must allow TCP/UDP 53 from on-premises.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The VPC's DNS support attribute is disabled…: DNS support must be enabled.
• The inbound endpoint is placed in a subnet…: Endpoints need network reachability.
• The private hosted zone is converted to a…: Public zones are not required.

Key takeaway: Check zone association and endpoint security groups.

stem: A network team wants VPCs, subnets, route tables, and transit gateway attachments deployed consistently across accounts. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Infrastructure as code with CloudFormation StackSets or Terraform through pipelines
A shared document listing settings that each account owner applies by hand
Copying screenshots of a reference VPC into each new account's wiki page
Manual configuration in the console by different engineers in each account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IaC deployed through pipelines ensures consistent network configuration across accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A shared document listing settings that each…: Documents do not enforce consistency.
• Copying screenshots of a reference VPC into…: Screenshots are not deployable.
• Manual configuration in the console by…: Manual setup drifts.

Key takeaway: Automate networks with IaC.

stem: When a new VPC attachment is created, it must be associated automatically with the correct transit gateway route table based on tags. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Asking application teams to email the network team after creating attachments
An EventBridge rule on attachment creation invoking a Lambda function that sets associations
A weekly review by the network team that fixes route table associations by hand
Enabling default route table association for every attachment in all environments

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Event-driven automation applies tag-based association rules as soon as attachments are created.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Asking application teams to email the…: Email requests are manual.
• A weekly review by the network team that…: Weekly reviews are slow.
• Enabling default route table association for…: Default association ignores environment segmentation.

Key takeaway: Automate TGW associations with events.

stem: A company wants a central dashboard of its global network topology, including transit gateways and on-premises sites. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Macie
AWS Artifact
AWS Cost Explorer
AWS Network Manager

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Network Manager visualizes and monitors global networks built on transit gateways and Cloud WAN.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Macie: Macie finds sensitive data.
• AWS Artifact: Artifact provides compliance documents.
• AWS Cost Explorer: Cost Explorer analyzes costs.

Key takeaway: Visualize global networks with Network Manager.

stem: A company wants on-premises applications to reach S3 over Direct Connect privately without traversing the internet. Which TWO options fit? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A Route 53 public hosted zone for S3 names
A second internet gateway on the same VPC
A private VIF to a VPC with an S3 interface endpoint
A NAT gateway in a public subnet of the VPC
A public VIF to reach S3 public endpoints over DX

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Public VIFs reach AWS public endpoints over DX, and interface endpoints expose S3 privately in a VPC reachable over a private VIF.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A Route 53 public hosted zone for S3 names: Public zones do not route traffic.
• A second internet gateway on the same VPC: A VPC has one IGW.
• A NAT gateway in a public subnet of the VPC: NAT gateways send traffic to the internet.

Key takeaway: Reach S3 over DX via public VIF or interface endpoints.

stem: EC2 instances in a private subnet must access S3 without NAT charges. Which endpoint type is the lowest-cost option?

choices.text: NAT gateway route
S3 interface endpoint
Internet gateway route
S3 gateway endpoint

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gateway endpoints for S3 have no hourly or data processing charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NAT gateway route: NAT adds charges.
• S3 interface endpoint: Interface endpoints have hourly and data charges.
• Internet gateway route: IGWs require public addressing.

Key takeaway: Lowest-cost private S3 access → gateway endpoint.

stem: On-premises clients over Direct Connect must reach S3 through a VPC endpoint. Why won't a gateway endpoint work?

choices.text: Gateway endpoints require a public VIF before they can be created
Gateway endpoints are reachable only from within the VPC, not from on-premises networks
Gateway endpoints support only DynamoDB traffic and never accept any S3 requests from clients
Gateway endpoints are regional and cannot be used by any EC2 instance

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gateway endpoints work through VPC route tables and cannot be reached from on-premises; interface endpoints can.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Gateway endpoints require a public VIF…: No public VIF is required.
• Gateway endpoints support only DynamoDB…: Gateway endpoints support S3 and DynamoDB.
• Gateway endpoints are regional and cannot be…: EC2 instances in the VPC use them.

Key takeaway: On-premises access to S3 via VPC → interface endpoints.

stem: A company uses Direct Connect and wants to use AWS BGP communities to control how far its routes are propagated within AWS on a public VIF. Which feature fits?

choices.text: MED values set on routes advertised to AWS over the VIF
Local preference communities on routes received from AWS
Scope communities such as 7224:9100 on advertised prefixes
AS_PATH prepending on routes advertised by AWS to customers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Public VIF scope communities (for example, 7224:9100 for the local Region) control propagation of customer routes within AWS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• MED values set on routes advertised to AWS…: MED is not used for scope control.
• Local preference communities on routes…: Local preference communities influence AWS's path selection on private or transit VIFs.
• AS_PATH prepending on routes advertised by…: Customers cannot prepend AWS's routes.

Key takeaway: Control public VIF route scope with communities.

stem: Instances in a VPC need IPv6 outbound internet access without allowing inbound IPv6 connections. Which component fits?

choices.text: Egress-only internet gateway
Transit gateway attachment only
NAT gateway in a public subnet
Virtual private gateway only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Egress-only internet gateways allow outbound IPv6 while blocking inbound connections.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transit gateway attachment only: TGWs route between networks.
• NAT gateway in a public subnet: NAT gateways are for IPv4 translation.
• Virtual private gateway only: VGWs connect VPNs.

Key takeaway: Outbound-only IPv6 → egress-only IGW.

stem: Resolver forwarding rules must be shared with 40 accounts in an OU. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Recreate the rules manually in each account
Put the rules in a public hosted zone
Share the rules with the OU through RAM
Copy the rules into DHCP option sets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RAM shares Resolver rules with accounts or OUs, which then associate them with VPCs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Recreate the rules manually in each account: Manual recreation drifts.
• Put the rules in a public hosted zone: Public zones are unrelated.
• Copy the rules into DHCP option sets: DHCP options do not contain Resolver rules.

Key takeaway: Share Resolver rules with RAM.

stem: Which TWO practices reduce risk when changing production routing through automation? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Validate changes with Reachability Analyzer before and after deployment
Disable monitoring during changes to reduce noise
Apply changes to all Regions at once during peak traffic
Make manual console edits after the automated deployment
Deploy changes in stages with automated rollback on health checks

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Pre and post checks and staged rollouts with rollback limit the impact of routing mistakes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable monitoring during changes to reduce…: Disabling monitoring hides problems.
• Apply changes to all Regions at once during…: Global simultaneous changes maximize blast radius.
• Make manual console edits after the…: Manual edits cause drift.

Key takeaway: Validate and stage network changes.

stem: Branch offices connect via VPN to a virtual private gateway and must also reach each other through AWS. Which feature enables this hub-and-spoke pattern?

choices.text: NAT gateways only
AWS VPN CloudHub
Gateway endpoints
VPC peering mesh

explanation:
Why this is correct:
VPN CloudHub lets multiple sites connected to a VGW communicate with each other.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NAT gateways only: NAT gateways provide egress.
• Gateway endpoints: Gateway endpoints access S3 and DynamoDB.
• VPC peering mesh: Peering connects VPCs.

Key takeaway: Site-to-site through a VGW → VPN CloudHub.

stem: Multicast traffic is required between EC2 instances across VPCs for a trading application. Which service supports this?

choices.text: VPC peering connections only
Amazon CloudFront distributions
Application Load Balancer rules
Transit Gateway multicast domains

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transit gateways support multicast domains for multicast traffic across attached VPCs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC peering connections only: Peering does not support multicast.
• Amazon CloudFront distributions: CloudFront delivers content.
• Application Load Balancer rules: ALBs route HTTP.

Key takeaway: Multicast in AWS → TGW multicast.

stem: After adding a new on-premises prefix, some routes are not reachable from AWS over a private VIF, and the BGP session flaps. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The security group on the instances allows all inbound traffic
The Direct Connect location changed its physical street address
The number of advertised prefixes exceeded the private VIF limit
The VPC's DHCP options set uses a custom domain name suffix

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Exceeding the private VIF prefix limit causes the BGP session to go down; summarizing routes fixes it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The security group on the instances allows…: Permissive security groups do not cause flapping.
• The Direct Connect location changed its…: Location addresses are irrelevant.
• The VPC's DHCP options set uses a custom…: DHCP options do not affect BGP.

Key takeaway: Summarize routes to stay under VIF prefix limits.

stem: A company must perform maintenance on its primary Direct Connect router without disrupting traffic. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Delete the private VIF and recreate it after the maintenance window ends
Change the VPC CIDR block so traffic reroutes automatically during work
Shut down the primary router immediately and wait for the BGP hold timers on both sides to expire naturally before starting work
Shift traffic to the backup path first, for example by prepending or lowering preference, then perform maintenance

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Draining traffic by adjusting BGP attributes before maintenance avoids disruption.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete the private VIF and recreate it after…: Deleting the VIF causes outages.
• Change the VPC CIDR block so traffic…: CIDR changes are disruptive and unrelated.
• Shut down the primary router immediately and…: Abrupt shutdowns cause loss until timers expire.

Key takeaway: Drain traffic before network maintenance.

stem: A company wants to test Direct Connect failover to its backup path in a controlled way. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Direct Connect failover testing that brings down BGP sessions temporarily
Physically unplugging cables without informing the team
Disabling the VPC's route table propagation permanently
Deleting the Direct Connect gateway and recreating it later once the test has finished

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Failover testing disables BGP sessions for a set duration so resiliency can be verified safely.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Physically unplugging cables without…: Uncoordinated unplugging is risky.
• Disabling the VPC's route table propagation…: Permanent changes break routing.
• Deleting the Direct Connect gateway and…: Deleting the gateway is disruptive.

Key takeaway: Validate DX resiliency with failover testing.

stem: Large packets over a VPN tunnel are dropped while small packets succeed. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: A route table that sends large packets to a different target
MTU and fragmentation issues; adjust MSS clamping or MTU on the tunnel
DNS resolution failures for the destination host name
Security groups that silently block large packets based on their total size in bytes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IPsec overhead reduces effective MTU; MSS clamping or MTU adjustments prevent drops.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A route table that sends large packets to a…: Route tables do not route by size.
• DNS resolution failures for the destination…: DNS failures affect all packets.
• Security groups that silently block large…: Security groups do not filter by size.

Key takeaway: Large-packet loss on tunnels → MTU and MSS settings.

stem: Within a VPC, instances exchange large data sets and the team wants to reduce packet overhead. What MTU do most current-generation instances support inside a VPC?

choices.text: 576 bytes only
65535 bytes on all paths
1024 bytes only
9001 bytes (jumbo frames)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Most current-generation instances support 9001-byte jumbo frames within a VPC.

Why the other options are wrong:
• 576 bytes only: 576 is a minimum IPv4 value.
• 65535 bytes on all paths: 65535 is not supported on network paths.
• 1024 bytes only: 1024 is not the VPC maximum.

Key takeaway: VPC jumbo frames → 9001 MTU.

stem: Traffic between an EC2 instance and the internet through an internet gateway fails with large packets after jumbo frames were enabled. What is the explanation?

choices.text: Jumbo frames are required for all internet traffic from AWS
Traffic leaving the VPC through an internet gateway is limited to 1500 bytes MTU
Internet gateways fragment every outbound packet into 64-byte segments before forwarding them
Internet gateways only accept packets smaller than 576 bytes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Paths outside the VPC, such as through an internet gateway, use a 1500-byte MTU.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Jumbo frames are required for all internet…: Jumbo frames are not used for internet traffic.
• Internet gateways fragment every outbound…: IGWs do not fragment into 64-byte segments.
• Internet gateways only accept packets…: 576 bytes is not the limit.

Key takeaway: Internet paths use a 1500-byte MTU.

stem: A team must find which source IP addresses generate the most rejected connections to a subnet over the past week. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Query VPC Flow Logs in S3 with Athena or use CloudWatch Logs Insights
Review CloudTrail management events for all of the EC2 API calls made last week
Inspect Route 53 health check results for the subnet
Check AWS Config configuration history for the subnet

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Flow Logs record rejected connections, and query tools aggregate them by source IP.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Review CloudTrail management events for all…: CloudTrail records API calls, not traffic.
• Inspect Route 53 health check results for…: Health checks monitor endpoints.
• Check AWS Config configuration history for…: Config records configuration changes.

Key takeaway: Analyze traffic patterns by querying Flow Logs.

stem: Which TWO Flow Log enhancements help analyze traffic through transit gateways and across AZs? (Select TWO)

choices.text: AWS Trusted Advisor checks
CloudTrail Insights on EC2 APIs
Custom Flow Log fields such as az-id and flow-direction
S3 Storage Lens dashboards
Transit Gateway Flow Logs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
TGW Flow Logs capture transit traffic, and custom fields add context such as AZ and direction.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Trusted Advisor checks: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations.
• CloudTrail Insights on EC2 APIs: Insights detects unusual API activity.
• S3 Storage Lens dashboards: Storage Lens reports S3 usage.

Key takeaway: Enrich traffic analysis with TGW Flow Logs and custom fields.

stem: A company wants to identify unintended network access paths, such as resources reachable from the internet, across its VPCs. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection
CloudWatch Synthetics canaries
Network Access Analyzer
Route 53 Resolver query logs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Network Access Analyzer identifies network paths that do not meet defined access requirements.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Cost Anomaly Detection: Cost anomaly detection watches spend.
• CloudWatch Synthetics canaries: Synthetics tests endpoints.
• Route 53 Resolver query logs: Query logs record DNS.

Key takeaway: Find unintended network paths with Network Access Analyzer.

stem: A team wants to monitor latency and packet loss between its on-premises sites and AWS Regions over the global network. Which feature fits?

choices.text: AWS Artifact reports about AWS network compliance
Network Manager infrastructure performance and CloudWatch network monitoring
S3 server access logs collected from the application buckets in each Region
IAM Access Analyzer findings for network roles

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Network Manager and CloudWatch network monitoring provide latency and loss metrics for network paths.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Artifact reports about AWS network…: Artifact provides compliance reports.
• S3 server access logs collected from the…: S3 access logs record requests.
• IAM Access Analyzer findings for network roles: Access Analyzer reviews permissions.

Key takeaway: Monitor network performance with Network Manager and CloudWatch.

stem: An NLB-backed service intermittently fails. Which TWO data sources help diagnose connection issues? (Select TWO)

choices.text: VPC Flow Logs on the NLB's network interfaces and targets
Route 53 public hosted zone change history
AWS Budgets forecast reports for networking
IAM credential report for all account users
NLB CloudWatch metrics such as TCP reset counts and healthy host count

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NLB metrics show resets and target health, and Flow Logs show accepted and rejected flows.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route 53 public hosted zone change history: Zone change history is unrelated.
• AWS Budgets forecast reports for networking: Budgets track spend.
• IAM credential report for all account users: Credential reports are unrelated.

Key takeaway: Diagnose NLB issues with metrics and Flow Logs.

stem: NAT gateway data processing charges are high because instances pull large amounts of data from S3 and DynamoDB. Which change reduces cost?

choices.text: Add more NAT gateways in the same Availability Zone
Increase the size of the NAT gateway's subnet range
Move instances into public subnets with public IPs
Add gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gateway endpoints avoid NAT processing charges for S3 and DynamoDB traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Add more NAT gateways in the same…: More NAT gateways add cost.
• Increase the size of the NAT gateway's…: Subnet size does not affect charges.
• Move instances into public subnets with…: Public subnets expose instances.

Key takeaway: Cut NAT costs with gateway endpoints.

stem: Cross-AZ data transfer charges are high between an application and its NLB targets. Which setting may reduce them?

choices.text: Use a Classic Load Balancer instead of the NLB for traffic
Disable cross-zone load balancing on the NLB if traffic is balanced per AZ
Enable cross-zone load balancing on the NLB for all of its target groups
Add targets in a third AZ that receives no client traffic

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With cross-zone disabled, NLB nodes send traffic to targets in their own AZ, avoiding inter-AZ charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Use a Classic Load Balancer instead of the…: Classic is legacy and not a cost fix.
• Enable cross-zone load balancing on the NLB…: Enabling cross-zone increases inter-AZ traffic.
• Add targets in a third AZ that receives no…: Extra AZ targets add cross-AZ traffic.

Key takeaway: Keep NLB traffic AZ-local to reduce transfer costs.

stem: A company wants higher single-flow throughput between instances. Which TWO actions help? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Send traffic over the public internet
Route traffic through a NAT gateway first
Place instances in a cluster placement group
Use smaller, previous-generation instances
Use instances with enhanced networking (ENA)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cluster placement groups and enhanced networking improve bandwidth and latency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Send traffic over the public internet: Internet paths reduce performance.
• Route traffic through a NAT gateway first: NAT adds a hop.
• Use smaller, previous-generation instances: Older instances have lower bandwidth.

Key takeaway: Maximize throughput with placement groups and ENA.

stem: A transit gateway processes large volumes of traffic between two VPCs that communicate heavily, adding cost. Which change can reduce cost?

choices.text: Increase the MTU on the transit gateway attachments to reduce charges
Move both VPCs to different Regions to reduce transit gateway usage
Add another transit gateway and route the same traffic through both of them
Add a VPC peering connection for that high-volume pair while keeping TGW for others

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Peering has no per-GB processing charge like TGW, so it can be cheaper for heavy pairwise traffic in the same Region.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Increase the MTU on the transit gateway…: MTU does not change charges.
• Move both VPCs to different Regions to…: Cross-Region traffic costs more.
• Add another transit gateway and route the…: Two TGWs add cost.

Key takeaway: Use peering for heavy pairwise traffic to save TGW costs.

stem: A company wants to improve availability of its hybrid DNS resolution. Which design fits?

choices.text: Resolver endpoints with IP addresses in at least two AZs
A single Resolver endpoint IP address in one AZ
One on-premises DNS server with no secondary server
DNS resolution over the public internet only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Multi-AZ endpoint IPs keep resolution available if an AZ fails.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A single Resolver endpoint IP address in one AZ: A single AZ is a single point of failure.
• One on-premises DNS server with no secondary…: One DNS server is a single point of failure.
• DNS resolution over the public internet only: Public resolution does not serve private zones.

Key takeaway: Deploy Resolver endpoints across AZs.

stem: CloudFront serves a global site, but the cache hit ratio is low because query strings with tracking parameters vary. Which change helps?

choices.text: Reduce the default TTL to zero for all objects in the distribution
Include all headers, cookies, and query strings in the cache key
Disable compression so that responses are cached more consistently
Use a cache policy that excludes unneeded query strings from the cache key

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Removing irrelevant values from the cache key increases cache hits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reduce the default TTL to zero for all…: Zero TTL disables caching.
• Include all headers, cookies, and query…: Including everything fragments the cache.
• Disable compression so that responses are…: Compression does not affect cache keys.

Key takeaway: Improve cache hit ratio with lean cache keys.

stem: An application's DNS failover takes too long because clients cache records. Which TWO actions reduce failover time? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Remove health checks to avoid false alarms
Use health checks with appropriate intervals and thresholds
Increase the TTL to one day for stability
Use a simple routing policy with one record
Lower the TTL on the failover records

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lower TTLs and responsive health checks make DNS failover faster.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove health checks to avoid false alarms: No health checks means no failover.
• Increase the TTL to one day for stability: Long TTLs delay failover.
• Use a simple routing policy with one record: Simple routing has no failover.

Key takeaway: Speed DNS failover with low TTLs and health checks.

stem: A team must confirm that a new security group rule actually allows traffic from an ALB to targets without sending test traffic. Which tool fits?

choices.text: VPC Reachability Analyzer
Amazon Inspector
AWS Artifact
CloudWatch Synthetics

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Reachability Analyzer analyzes configurations to verify paths.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Inspector: Inspector finds vulnerabilities.
• AWS Artifact: Artifact provides compliance documents.
• CloudWatch Synthetics: Synthetics sends real requests.

Key takeaway: Verify paths without traffic using Reachability Analyzer.

stem: Instances in a private subnet cannot reach the internet. The route table has 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway. Which TWO issues could cause this? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The VPC has DNS hostnames enabled by default
The instances have too much memory allocated
The NAT gateway is in a subnet without a route to the internet gateway
The instances use an Amazon Linux AMI
NACLs block return traffic on ephemeral ports

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The NAT gateway's subnet must route to the IGW, and NACLs must allow return traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The VPC has DNS hostnames enabled by default: DNS hostnames do not block egress.
• The instances have too much memory allocated: Memory is unrelated.
• The instances use an Amazon Linux AMI: The AMI is unrelated.

Key takeaway: Check NAT subnet routing and NACL ephemeral ports.

stem: A NAT gateway occasionally reports ErrorPortAllocation because many connections target the same destination. Which change helps?

choices.text: Move the NAT gateway into a private subnet without a route
Reduce the number of private subnets that route through the NAT gateway to just one
Add secondary IP addresses to the NAT gateway or spread traffic across NAT gateways
Disable DNS support on the VPC to reduce connection counts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
More source IPs increase available ports for connections to the same destination.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Move the NAT gateway into a private subnet…: A NAT gateway in a private subnet cannot reach the internet.
• Reduce the number of private subnets that…: Fewer subnets does not add ports.
• Disable DNS support on the VPC to reduce…: DNS settings do not affect ports.

Key takeaway: Fix port exhaustion with more NAT source IPs.

stem: A company wants alerts when Direct Connect connection state changes or BGP goes down. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Route 53 query logging on the on-premises domain names
CloudWatch alarms on Direct Connect metrics such as ConnectionState and BGP status
A weekly manual login to the Direct Connect console by an engineer who checks each connection
S3 event notifications on the bucket storing router backups

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Direct Connect publishes CloudWatch metrics, including connection and BGP states, for alarms.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route 53 query logging on the on-premises…: Query logs are unrelated.
• A weekly manual login to the Direct Connect…: Weekly checks are too slow.
• S3 event notifications on the bucket storing…: S3 events are unrelated.

Key takeaway: Alarm on Direct Connect health metrics.

stem: A company must filter outbound traffic from VPCs so that only approved domains are reachable, with stateful inspection. Which service fits?

choices.text: An internet gateway with a restrictive route table
Network ACLs with deny rules for unknown domains
Security groups with outbound rules by domain name
AWS Network Firewall with domain list rule groups

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Network Firewall supports stateful domain filtering for egress traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An internet gateway with a restrictive route…: IGWs do not filter.
• Network ACLs with deny rules for unknown domains: NACLs are stateless and IP-based.
• Security groups with outbound rules by…: Security groups filter by IP and port, not domain.

Key takeaway: Domain-based egress control → Network Firewall.

stem: A company needs intrusion prevention with Suricata-compatible rules for traffic between VPCs. Which design fits?

choices.text: Network Firewall in an inspection VPC with transit gateway routing and appliance mode
A single EC2 proxy instance handling all traffic in one AZ
NACLs on each subnet with stateless allow rules for all traffic
Security groups on every instance, with broad allow rules for traffic from all of the other VPCs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Network Firewall supports Suricata rules, and centralized inspection with TGW covers east-west traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A single EC2 proxy instance handling all…: A single proxy is a bottleneck and single point of failure.
• NACLs on each subnet with stateless allow…: NACLs do not provide IPS.
• Security groups on every instance, with…: Security groups do not provide IPS.

Key takeaway: Centralized IPS → Network Firewall inspection VPC.

stem: A web application must be protected from SQL injection and rate-limited per IP. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS WAF with managed rules and rate-based rules
Network ACLs with port restrictions only
AWS Shield Standard default protections
VPC Flow Logs with alerts on traffic

explanation:
Why this is correct:
WAF inspects HTTP requests and enforces rate limits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Network ACLs with port restrictions only: NACLs cannot inspect HTTP.
• AWS Shield Standard default protections: Shield Standard protects against network DDoS.
• VPC Flow Logs with alerts on traffic: Flow Logs do not block.

Key takeaway: Web attacks and rate limits → WAF.

stem: A company must protect public applications against large DDoS attacks, with cost protection and access to the response team. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS WAF alone
Security groups only
Amazon GuardDuty only
AWS Shield Advanced

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced adds enhanced DDoS protection, cost protection, and response team access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS WAF alone: WAF filters requests but is not full DDoS protection.
• Security groups only: Security groups do not mitigate DDoS.
• Amazon GuardDuty only: GuardDuty detects threats.

Key takeaway: Advanced DDoS protection → Shield Advanced.

stem: Security groups in a VPC must allow traffic from instances in a peered VPC in the same Region by referencing their security group. Is this possible?

choices.text: No, peered VPCs cannot exchange any traffic at all
Yes, but only when the VPCs are in different AWS Regions
Yes, security groups can reference groups in peered VPCs in the same Region
No, security groups can only reference CIDR blocks, never groups

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security groups can reference security groups in peered VPCs within the same Region.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No, peered VPCs cannot exchange any traffic…: Peered VPCs can exchange traffic.
• Yes, but only when the VPCs are in different…: Cross-Region peering does not support references.
• No, security groups can only reference CIDR…: Group references are supported.

Key takeaway: Reference peered security groups within a Region.

stem: Which TWO controls are stateless and evaluated at the subnet boundary? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Security group outbound rules
Network ACL inbound rules
Security group inbound rules
AWS WAF web ACL rules
Network ACL outbound rules

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Network ACLs are stateless subnet-level controls with separate inbound and outbound rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Security group outbound rules: Security groups are stateful.
• Security group inbound rules: Security groups are stateful and apply to interfaces.
• AWS WAF web ACL rules: WAF applies to web requests at supported resources.

Key takeaway: NACLs are stateless; security groups are stateful.

stem: Auditors require evidence of all network configuration changes, such as route table and security group edits, with the user identity. Which TWO sources fit? (Select TWO)

choices.text: VPC Flow Logs only
CloudFront access logs
AWS CloudTrail
S3 Storage Lens
AWS Config history

explanation:
Why this is correct:

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC Flow Logs only: Flow Logs record traffic, not changes.
• CloudFront access logs: CloudFront logs record requests.
• S3 Storage Lens: Storage Lens reports usage.

Key takeaway: Audit network changes with CloudTrail and Config.

stem: A company must continuously check that no security group allows unrestricted SSH and automatically remediate violations. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A monthly report exported from the console and reviewed by hand by the network team
CloudFront geo restriction applied to the SSH port traffic
VPC Flow Logs stored in S3 without any analysis configured
AWS Config rule with automatic remediation using an SSM Automation document

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Config detects noncompliant rules, and automatic remediation removes them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A monthly report exported from the console…: Monthly reviews are slow.
• CloudFront geo restriction applied to the…: CloudFront does not control SSH.
• VPC Flow Logs stored in S3 without any…: Stored logs without analysis do nothing.

Key takeaway: Continuously enforce security group rules with Config.

stem: A company must centrally manage WAF rules, Shield Advanced protections, and security group policies across accounts. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Firewall Manager
AWS Security Hub
AWS Config only
Amazon Detective

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Firewall Manager centrally applies firewall policies across accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Security Hub: Security Hub aggregates findings.
• AWS Config only: Config evaluates but does not deploy firewall rules.
• Amazon Detective: Detective investigates.

Key takeaway: Central firewall policies → Firewall Manager.

stem: Network Firewall must log alerts and flows to a central location for analysis. Which destinations can be configured?

choices.text: Only a local disk on the firewall endpoint
S3, CloudWatch Logs, or Data Firehose
Only email notifications sent to the team
Only DynamoDB tables in the same account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Network Firewall logs can be delivered to S3, CloudWatch Logs, or Firehose.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only a local disk on the firewall endpoint: There is no local disk option.
• Only email notifications sent to the team: Email is not a log destination.
• Only DynamoDB tables in the same account: DynamoDB is not a direct destination.

Key takeaway: Send firewall logs to S3, CloudWatch Logs, or Firehose.

stem: A company needs to detect threats such as communication with known malicious IPs from its VPCs. Which service analyzes Flow Logs and DNS logs for this?

choices.text: Amazon GuardDuty
Amazon Inspector
AWS Firewall Manager
AWS Shield Standard

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty analyzes VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs, and CloudTrail to detect threats.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Inspector: Inspector scans vulnerabilities.
• AWS Firewall Manager: Firewall Manager manages policies.
• AWS Shield Standard: Shield Standard mitigates DDoS.

Key takeaway: Network threat detection → GuardDuty.

stem: Traffic between an ALB and targets must be encrypted end to end. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: TCP listener on an ALB with no certificates at all
HTTP listener on the ALB and HTTP target group to targets
HTTPS listener on the ALB and HTTPS target group with certificates on targets
HTTPS listener on the ALB, with an HTTP target group forwarding plain traffic to the targets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Re-encrypting to targets with HTTPS keeps traffic encrypted end to end.

Why the other options are wrong:
• TCP listener on an ALB with no certificates…: ALBs do not offer TCP listeners.
• HTTP listener on the ALB and HTTP target…: No encryption at all.
• HTTPS listener on the ALB, with an HTTP…: Backend HTTP is unencrypted.

Key takeaway: End-to-end TLS through ALB → HTTPS to targets.

stem: Clients must connect with TLS to an NLB, and the backend must receive decrypted traffic with centralized certificate management. Which option fits?

choices.text: NLB TCP listener with certificates on clients
NLB TLS listener with an ACM certificate
ALB with HTTP listeners only for all traffic
Global Accelerator with no certificates

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NLB TLS listeners terminate TLS using ACM certificates.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NLB TCP listener with certificates on clients: TCP listeners pass through encrypted traffic without termination.
• ALB with HTTP listeners only for all traffic: HTTP listeners are unencrypted.
• Global Accelerator with no certificates: Global Accelerator does not terminate TLS.

Key takeaway: Terminate TLS on NLB with ACM.

stem: A company needs private certificates for internal services with automated issuance and renewal. Which service fits?

choices.text: Self-signed certificates on each host
Route 53 DNSSEC keys
Public ACM certificates only
AWS Private Certificate Authority

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Private CA issues private certificates, and ACM can manage their renewal.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Self-signed certificates on each host: Self-signed certificates are hard to manage.
• Route 53 DNSSEC keys: DNSSEC keys sign DNS.
• Public ACM certificates only: Public certificates are for public domains.

Key takeaway: Private PKI → AWS Private CA.

stem: Which TWO options encrypt traffic between on-premises and AWS? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Jumbo frames on the Direct Connect link
VPC peering between on-premises and AWS
A private VIF without any additional configuration
MACsec on supported Direct Connect connections
Site-to-Site VPN over the internet or over Direct Connect

explanation:
Why this is correct:
VPN encrypts with IPsec, and MACsec encrypts at layer 2 on supported DX connections.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Jumbo frames on the Direct Connect link: MTU does not encrypt.
• VPC peering between on-premises and AWS: Peering does not connect on-premises.
• A private VIF without any additional…: A private VIF alone is not encrypted.

Key takeaway: Encrypt hybrid traffic with VPN or MACsec.

stem: Employees need access to internal web applications without a VPN, with identity and device posture checks. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Verified Access
AWS Client VPN only
AWS Direct Connect
Amazon CloudFront

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Verified Access provides zero-trust, VPN-less access with identity and device checks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Client VPN only: Client VPN is VPN-based.
• AWS Direct Connect: Direct Connect is private connectivity.
• Amazon CloudFront: CloudFront is a CDN.

Key takeaway: VPN-less zero-trust access → Verified Access.

stem: Remote employees need secure access to VPC resources using an OpenVPN-based client with Active Directory authentication. Which service fits?

choices.text: Transit Gateway
AWS Client VPN
Internet Gateway
Site-to-Site VPN

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Client VPN is a managed OpenVPN-based service supporting AD and SAML authentication.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transit Gateway: TGW routes between networks.
• Internet Gateway: IGWs provide internet access.
• Site-to-Site VPN: Site-to-Site VPN connects networks.

Key takeaway: Remote user VPN → Client VPN.

stem: An organization wants to prevent any account from creating internet gateways except in approved networking accounts. Which control fits?

choices.text: A weekly script that finds and deletes any internet gateways created in member accounts
A security group rule that blocks all traffic to internet gateways
An SCP denying ec2:CreateInternetGateway and attachment actions outside approved accounts
A Route 53 policy that prevents public DNS records for all accounts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SCPs prevent creating or attaching internet gateways in non-approved accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A weekly script that finds and deletes any…: Deleting afterward allows exposure windows.
• A security group rule that blocks all…: Security groups do not stop IGW creation.
• A Route 53 policy that prevents public DNS…: DNS policies are unrelated.

Key takeaway: Prevent unapproved internet paths with SCPs.

stem: Access to an S3 bucket must be allowed only through a specific VPC endpoint. Which control fits?

choices.text: A NACL on the subnet that blocks S3 IPs
A security group attached to the S3 bucket
A Route 53 private zone for the S3 name
A bucket policy with an aws:SourceVpce condition

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bucket policies with aws:SourceVpce restrict access to requests through the endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A NACL on the subnet that blocks S3 IPs: NACLs do not reliably target S3.
• A security group attached to the S3 bucket: S3 buckets have no security groups.
• A Route 53 private zone for the S3 name: DNS zones do not enforce access.

Key takeaway: Restrict S3 to endpoints with SourceVpce conditions.

stem: A VPC endpoint for S3 must allow access only to the company's own buckets to prevent data exfiltration. Which control fits?

choices.text: Public IP addresses on the instances
A second internet gateway on the VPC
A VPC endpoint policy restricting resources to company buckets
A larger VPC CIDR block for the subnets that use the endpoint

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Endpoint policies limit which buckets can be accessed through the endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public IP addresses on the instances: Public IPs increase exposure.
• A second internet gateway on the VPC: A VPC has one IGW.
• A larger VPC CIDR block for the subnets that…: CIDR size is unrelated.

Key takeaway: Prevent exfiltration with endpoint policies.

stem: A company must store VPC Flow Logs for one year in a tamper-resistant way for compliance. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Keep Flow Logs in CloudWatch Logs with a seven-day retention period
Deliver Flow Logs to an S3 bucket in a log archive account with Object Lock
Store Flow Logs on an EBS volume attached to a logging instance
Disable Flow Logs and rely on CloudTrail for traffic information

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Central S3 storage with Object Lock meets retention and tamper-resistance needs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Keep Flow Logs in CloudWatch Logs with a…: Seven days is too short.
• Store Flow Logs on an EBS volume attached to…: EBS can be modified or lost.
• Disable Flow Logs and rely on CloudTrail for…: CloudTrail does not record traffic.

Key takeaway: Retain network logs immutably in a log archive account.

stem: A company wants service-to-service authorization based on IAM identities for HTTP traffic between microservices in different VPCs. Which option fits?

choices.text: VPC Lattice with auth policies using IAM
Security groups with CIDR-based rules only
NACLs with stateless allow rules only
Public ALBs with no authentication

explanation:
Why this is correct:
VPC Lattice auth policies authorize requests based on IAM identities.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Security groups with CIDR-based rules only: CIDR rules are not identity-based.
• NACLs with stateless allow rules only: NACLs are not identity-based.
• Public ALBs with no authentication: Public ALBs without auth are insecure.

Key takeaway: Identity-based service authorization → VPC Lattice.

stem: DNS queries from VPCs must be protected from exfiltration through suspicious domains. Which TWO controls help? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Disabling DNS support in the VPCs
Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall with block lists
Public hosted zones for all domains
Longer TTLs on all DNS records
GuardDuty monitoring of DNS logs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DNS Firewall blocks known bad domains, and GuardDuty detects suspicious DNS activity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disabling DNS support in the VPCs: Disabling DNS breaks workloads.
• Public hosted zones for all domains: Public zones do not block queries.
• Longer TTLs on all DNS records: TTLs are unrelated.

Key takeaway: Protect DNS with DNS Firewall and GuardDuty.

stem: An organization must verify that no VPC in any account has routes to the internet from subnets tagged 'restricted'. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Network Access Analyzer scopes run across accounts with findings reviewed
Cost Explorer reports filtered by data transfer charges
CloudFront access logs analyzed for unusual requests
Manual inspection of every route table in each account by network engineers each quarter

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Network Access Analyzer evaluates network paths against defined scopes to find violations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cost Explorer reports filtered by data…: Cost reports do not verify paths.
• CloudFront access logs analyzed for unusual…: CloudFront logs are unrelated.
• Manual inspection of every route table in…: Manual inspection does not scale.

Key takeaway: Verify network isolation requirements with Network Access Analyzer.

stem: A company wants to block traffic from specific countries to its web application at the edge. Which TWO options fit? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Route 53 simple routing policies
Security groups with country filters
CloudFront geo restrictions
NACLs with country-based rules
AWS WAF geo match rules

explanation:
Why this is correct:
WAF geo match and CloudFront geo restrictions block by country.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route 53 simple routing policies: Simple routing does not block.
• Security groups with country filters: Security groups do not filter by country.
• NACLs with country-based rules: NACLs do not filter by country.

Key takeaway: Block countries with WAF or CloudFront geo restrictions.

stem: A company needs to encrypt traffic between EC2 instances in a VPC without application changes, on supported instance types. Which fact applies?

choices.text: Encryption is only possible when using public IP addresses
All VPC traffic between instances is always sent in clear text, with no encryption options available
Encryption requires routing all traffic through a NAT gateway
Supported Nitro instance types automatically encrypt in-transit traffic between them

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Certain Nitro-based instance types automatically encrypt traffic between supported instances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Encryption is only possible when using…: Public IPs do not encrypt.
• All VPC traffic between instances is always…: Encryption options exist.
• Encryption requires routing all traffic…: NAT does not encrypt.

Key takeaway: Nitro instances can encrypt in-transit traffic automatically.

stem: An application needs WebSocket connections behind a load balancer with HTTP routing rules. Which option fits?

choices.text: Gateway Load Balancer
Application Load Balancer
VPC endpoint service
Classic Load Balancer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ALB supports WebSocket connections and HTTP routing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Gateway Load Balancer: GWLB is for appliances.
• VPC endpoint service: Endpoint services expose services via PrivateLink.
• Classic Load Balancer: Classic is legacy.

Key takeaway: WebSockets with HTTP routing → ALB.

stem: Users should be routed to the Region with the lowest network latency. Which Route 53 policy fits?

choices.text: Simple routing
Geolocation routing
Weighted routing
Latency-based routing

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Latency routing selects the Region with the lowest measured latency for the user.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Simple routing: Simple routing returns one record set.
• Geolocation routing: Geolocation routes by location, not latency.
• Weighted routing: Weighted splits traffic by weight.

Key takeaway: Lowest latency → latency routing.

stem: A VPC needs a custom domain suffix and specific DNS servers for its instances. Which feature fits?

choices.text: A DHCP options set
An endpoint policy
A route table
A prefix list

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DHCP options sets configure domain name and DNS servers for instances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An endpoint policy: Endpoint policies control endpoint access.
• A route table: Route tables direct traffic.
• A prefix list: Prefix lists group CIDRs.

Key takeaway: Customize VPC DNS settings with DHCP options sets.

stem: A company wants a record of all changes to Network Firewall rule groups for compliance audits. Which TWO sources fit? (Select TWO)

choices.text: CloudFront access logs for the web application
Route 53 query logs for the firewall subnets
CloudTrail events for Network Firewall API calls
VPC Flow Logs for the firewall endpoints only
AWS Config configuration history for rule groups

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudTrail records who changed rules, and Config tracks rule group configuration over time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFront access logs for the web application: CloudFront logs record requests.
• Route 53 query logs for the firewall subnets: Query logs record DNS.
• VPC Flow Logs for the firewall endpoints only: Flow Logs record traffic.

Key takeaway: Audit firewall rule changes with CloudTrail and Config.

stem: A private API must be accessible only from specific VPCs through interface endpoints. Which TWO controls fit? (Select TWO)

choices.text: An internet gateway attached to every consumer VPC
An API Gateway private API with a resource policy restricting source VPC endpoints
A public REST API with an IP allow list for the VPC CIDRs
A public DNS record pointing to the private API
Interface VPC endpoints for execute-api in the allowed VPCs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Private APIs with resource policies limit access to specific endpoints, reachable via interface endpoints.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An internet gateway attached to every…: IGWs are unnecessary.
• A public REST API with an IP allow list for…: Public APIs are internet-facing.
• A public DNS record pointing to the private API: Public DNS does not provide access control.

Key takeaway: Restrict private APIs to specific VPC endpoints.

stem: A company runs a web application on an Application Load Balancer that must stay internal, with no public IP addresses and no internet gateway route to its subnets. The company now wants to put Amazon CloudFront in front of the application for caching and AWS WAF protection. Which design meets these requirements with the least operational effort?

choices.text: Make the ALB internet-facing, then restrict its security group to the CloudFront origin-facing managed prefix list and require a secret custom origin header
Place an internet-facing Network Load Balancer with IP targets in front of the internal ALB and use the NLB DNS name as the CloudFront custom origin
Create a CloudFront VPC origin that points to the internal ALB, so CloudFront reaches it privately through the VPC without making the load balancer internet-facing
Configure origin access control (OAC) on the distribution for the internal ALB so that CloudFront signs every origin request with SigV4 credentials

explanation:
## How CloudFront normally reaches a custom origin
A classic custom origin (ALB, EC2, on-premises server) is reached over the public internet: CloudFront resolves the origin's DNS name and connects to a public IP. To keep others out, teams lock the origin down with the `com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing` managed prefix list and a secret header, but the origin is still internet-facing.
## CloudFront VPC origins
A **VPC origin** lets CloudFront deliver from an ALB, NLB or EC2 instance that sits in a **private subnet**. CloudFront creates service-managed network interfaces in your VPC and connects to the origin privately, so:
- the origin needs no public IP and its subnets need no route to an internet gateway (the VPC itself must still have an internet gateway attached);
- the only way in is through the distribution, where AWS WAF, caching and geo rules apply;
- there is no prefix list or shared-secret header to maintain.
Example: `internal-app-123.eu-west-1.elb.amazonaws.com` becomes a VPC origin, and the security group on the ALB allows the CloudFront VPC origin traffic only.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Internet-facing ALB with prefix list:** this is the older lockdown pattern, but it breaks the stated requirement that the ALB have no public addresses, and the secret header must be rotated and managed.
- ✗ **B. Public NLB in front of the ALB:** this reintroduces an internet-facing entry point with public IPs, adds a second load balancer to operate, and anyone who finds the NLB name can bypass CloudFront and WAF.
- ✓ **C. CloudFront VPC origin (correct):** it is built for exactly this case, delivering from an internal ALB in private subnets, so the load balancer never becomes internet-facing and all traffic is forced through CloudFront and AWS WAF.
- ✗ **D. Origin access control:** OAC signs requests to AWS origins such as Amazon S3, MediaStore or Lambda function URLs. It does not give CloudFront a network path into a VPC, so an internal ALB would still be unreachable.

## Key idea
To front a private ALB, NLB or EC2 origin with CloudFront, use a VPC origin; prefix lists and secret headers only harden an origin that is still public.

stem: A retailer wants to test a new CloudFront configuration (different cache policy and a new origin request policy) on a small share of real production traffic before promoting it, and must be able to roll back in seconds without changing DNS. QA engineers must also be able to force their own requests onto the new configuration. Which approach fits best?

choices.text: Use CloudFront continuous deployment with a staging distribution and a continuous deployment policy, using weight-based routing for users and a header-based policy for QA requests
Deploy a Lambda@Edge viewer request function that randomly rewrites 5 percent of requests to a second cache behavior that carries the new policies and origin settings
Add a new cache behavior with the new policies to the existing distribution and let CloudFront shift traffic to it gradually using the behavior precedence order
Create a second distribution with the new settings and use Route 53 weighted records to send 5 percent of viewers to its domain name, lowering the weight to zero to roll back

explanation:
## Why testing CloudFront changes is hard
A distribution change propagates to every edge location and applies to all viewers. A bad cache policy can hurt the cache hit ratio or break an application for everyone at once.
## Continuous deployment
CloudFront **continuous deployment** pairs a **primary distribution** with a **staging distribution** that holds the candidate configuration. A **continuous deployment policy** on the primary decides which requests go to staging:
- **Weight-based**: a small percentage of viewer requests (up to 15 percent) goes to staging, optionally with session stickiness so one user stays on one configuration.
- **Header-based**: requests that carry a specific header (the name must start with `aws-cf-cd-`, for example `aws-cf-cd-qa: true`) always go to staging.
Viewers keep using the same domain name. When the test succeeds you **promote** the staging configuration into the primary; to roll back you disable or change the policy, and no DNS change is needed.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Continuous deployment with a staging distribution (correct):** the policy splits a small weight of production traffic onto the new configuration with no DNS change, a header-based rule lets QA force requests onto staging, and promotion or rollback is a policy action.
- ✗ **B. Random rewrite in Lambda@Edge:** the cache behavior is matched before its viewer request function runs, so rewriting the URI does not move the request onto another behavior's policies; the custom code also adds latency and cost to every request.
- ✗ **C. Behavior precedence:** cache behaviors are matched by path pattern in a fixed order. CloudFront never shifts a percentage of traffic between behaviors, so this cannot run a gradual test.
- ✗ **D. Route 53 weights across two distributions:** this changes DNS, so rollback waits on resolver and client caching of the records, and QA cannot pin their requests to the new configuration by header.

## Key idea
Canary-test CloudFront settings with continuous deployment (staging distribution + weight or header policy), not with DNS weights or edge code.

stem: A CloudFront distribution in front of an ALB serves a product catalog. The origin needs the CloudFront-Viewer-Country header and a session cookie to build personalized logs, but responses are identical for all viewers. After the team added these values to the cache policy, the cache hit ratio fell sharply. What should the team change?

choices.text: Keep the header and cookie in the cache policy but raise the minimum TTL so that cached objects stay at edge locations longer and fewer requests reach the ALB
Enable Origin Shield in the Region closest to the ALB so that the extra cache variations are consolidated in one regional layer before reaching the origin
Move the personalization logic into a CloudFront Function that strips the header and cookie from viewer requests before the cache lookup happens
Remove the values from the cache policy and add them to an origin request policy, so CloudFront forwards them to the origin without including them in the cache key

explanation:
## Cache key versus origin request
CloudFront uses two separate policies on each cache behavior:
- A **cache policy** defines the **cache key**: the URL plus any headers, cookies and query strings you list. Every distinct combination is stored as a separate object. Values in the cache key are also forwarded to the origin automatically.
- An **origin request policy** lists values CloudFront should **send to the origin on a cache miss** without adding them to the cache key.
## Why the hit ratio dropped
A session cookie is unique per user and `CloudFront-Viewer-Country` has many values. Putting them in the cache key splits one catalog page into thousands of cache entries, so almost every request misses.
Example: `/catalog/shoes` with 50,000 active sessions becomes 50,000 separate cached objects, although the content is the same.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Longer minimum TTL:** each cache entry lives longer, but there are still thousands of entries per page because every session value is a separate key, so most requests keep missing.
- ✗ **B. Origin Shield:** it adds a central caching layer, but it uses the same cache key, so every unique cookie still creates a separate object and the hit ratio stays low.
- ✗ **C. Strip values in a CloudFront Function:** removing the header and cookie before the cache lookup also removes them from the origin request, so the origin would lose the data it needs for its logs.
- ✓ **D. Origin request policy (correct):** it sends the country header and cookie to the ALB on cache misses while keeping the cache key to the URL, so identical responses are shared by all viewers again.

## Key idea
Values the origin needs but that do not change the response belong in the origin request policy; only values that change the response belong in the cache policy.

stem: A streaming company partners with three internet service providers. Subscribers on each ISP's network must be sent to a cache cluster hosted inside that ISP, identified by the ISP's published IP ranges, while everyone else uses the default CloudFront endpoint. Which Route 53 configuration fits?

choices.text: Geolocation routing records with one record per country served by each ISP, plus a default location record that points to the CloudFront distribution
Latency-based routing records with health checks, so that each subscriber reaches whichever ISP cache cluster answers fastest from its resolver
IP-based routing with a CIDR collection holding each ISP's ranges as locations, plus a default record for all other clients pointing to CloudFront
Geoproximity routing with a positive bias for each ISP cluster location, so that its area of influence covers the ISP's subscriber regions

explanation:
## Routing by who is asking
Most Route 53 policies route by **where** the resolver or client appears to be: geolocation (country or continent), geoproximity (distance with bias) or latency (measured to AWS Regions). None of them knows which network a client belongs to.
## IP-based routing
**IP-based routing** routes by the client's IP address, using the resolver IP or, when the resolver sends it, the EDNS Client Subnet.
- You create a **CIDR collection** and add **CIDR locations**, for example `isp-a` holding `198.51.100.0/22` and `203.0.113.0/24`.
- Each record set references a location, so `isp-a` answers with the IP of the cache inside ISP A.
- A record for the default location (`*`) answers everyone who matches no CIDR block.
This is the standard way to steer users of a known network, such as an ISP or a corporate range, to specific endpoints.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Geolocation per country:** all three ISPs can serve the same country, so a country-level rule cannot tell their subscribers apart and would send every ISP's users to one cluster.
- ✗ **B. Latency-based routing:** latency records must be tied to AWS Regions and measure latency to those Regions, not to caches hosted inside ISP networks, and they ignore which ISP the user belongs to.
- ✓ **C. IP-based routing with a CIDR collection (correct):** it matches the source address against each ISP's published ranges and answers with that ISP's cache, while the default location sends every other client to CloudFront.
- ✗ **D. Geoproximity with bias:** bias moves geographic boundaries between locations; ISPs overlap in the same areas, so distance-based regions cannot separate subscribers by their provider's IP ranges.

## Key idea
Route by the client's network (known CIDR ranges) with IP-based routing and CIDR collections; geolocation, geoproximity and latency only know location.

stem: A team enables query logging for a public hosted zone to measure how many DNS queries each record receives. The log group was created in eu-west-1, where the application runs, and nothing is logged. After fixing that, the query counts are far lower than the number of client requests the application sees. Which explanation covers both observations?

choices.text: Query logs for public hosted zones must go to a CloudWatch Logs log group in us-east-1, and only queries that reach Route 53 are logged, because DNS resolvers cache answers for the record TTL
Query logs for public hosted zones are delivered only to Amazon S3 buckets in the application's own Region, and Route 53 samples about one query in ten to keep the log volume under control
The log group needs a KMS key shared with Route 53 in the application Region, and queries for alias records are never logged because alias targets are resolved internally
Public hosted zone query logging requires Route 53 Resolver query logging to be enabled in each client VPC, and queries answered from Resolver endpoints are counted separately

explanation:
## Two different DNS logs
- **Resolver query logging** records queries made by resources inside your VPCs to the Route 53 Resolver.
- **Public DNS query logging** records queries that the Route 53 authoritative name servers receive for a **public hosted zone** from resolvers on the internet.
## Rules for public query logging
- Logs go only to **CloudWatch Logs**, and the log group must be in **us-east-1**. You also add a resource policy that lets Route 53 write to it.
- Each entry shows the query name, type, response code, the edge location that answered and the resolver IP.
## Why counts look low
Clients do not ask Route 53 directly. They ask a recursive resolver (an ISP or public resolver), which **caches** the answer for the record's TTL. With a TTL of 300 seconds, one resolver may send one query to Route 53 while thousands of its users connect to your app. Query logs therefore show resolver queries, not user visits.

## Why each option works or fails
